Doubts are entertained with regard to the probable ship that will bring out the European Mails of the 17th inst. The Parana, Captain Rivett, which left this port on the night of the 2nd July, could not have got home in sufficient time to be made ready to return hither with the mails of the 17th of the same month. The La Plata we know had not gone round to Southampton from Greenock on the 2nd, the day of departure of the Magdalcna from the former place. The mails, then, will most likely be brought, out either by the Thames, which left here on the 23rd ultimo, and no doubt arrived at Southampton about the 10th instant, þÿ affording her ample time to be got ready, or the Tay ; but if the latter ship could not be spared from the Brazilian route, there would be no other to fall back upon, and one would have to be chartered for the voyage. We, however, feel satisfied that the Thames will be the ship of the 17th, and may be looked for here about the 3d or 4th prox. The La Plata or Parana will follow with the mails of 2nd August. The Conway, Avon and Clyde drere all in dock undergoing repairs and improvements at the departure of the last Steamer.

In our present impression will be found a letter from the Jamaica Delegation now in London, to the people of Jamaica, addressed through John Nethersole, Esquire, Treasurer of the Delegation Fund in that Island, and also an Address of the Delegation to the inhabitants of the British West India Colonies. We commend these articles to the attentive perusal of our readers ; and we earnestly press the general subject upon their attention. We know not with what consistency complaints may be made of the distress which has befallen us, while we neglect the important measures which can alone be made effectual for accomplishing our amelioration. We here allude to the public at large. The House of Assembly lias acted wisely and well ; but its efforts have been neutralized bv the Council. It, therefore, de-

volves upon the people to support their representatives, and to make an effort which will in no wise be controlled by the caprice of a numerically insignificant coterie. Let us follow the example of our indefatigable and spirited neighbours of Jamaica, who, when the legislature, trampelled by partizanship, was unable to mature the project of a delegation, took the business into their own hands, raised the necessary means by spontaneous subscription, nominated their delegates by popular acclamation, and hurried them away to England. We, in Antigua, stand in a parallel position. The House of Assembly, vetoed by the Council, is unable to carry out its own and the people's design. Let. the people, then, take the matter, into their own hands. Let them in common convention consider and perfect such measures as shall give them a representation þÿ although not within the walls of Parliament, yet within an effective sphere þÿ in the approaching crisis at home. We must lie up and doing. The public meeting suggested through the columns of the press, is imperatively demanded, and should be called the are our public men dreaming? We take the li- ## berty of rousing them from their lethargy. # # # # "# We call upon men of intelligence, position, and influence, to form themselves into a committee without delay, for the purpose of taking the preliminary steps for this important measure. In Jamaica, the bench, the bar, the pulpit, the press, the counting-room, the plough, thus

combined in the initiatory step of seeking the deliverance of their ruined country; þÿ and the noble example thus established is worthy of the exercise of every muscle and sinew which our lesser Island possesses. Our more powerful has opened the way þÿ and a valiant leadership is calling upon us to follow. " We are now laying the foundation," say the Jamaica Delegates, in their appeal to these Islands, "and we " "suggest " cert " work which Jamaica carry lecting qualified persons to act in con- with us, and to the expediency of your se- has commenced." through the These delegates arc labouring, not for Jamaica only, but for us as well. In England, the word Jamaica frequency implies the whole British West Indies þÿ and relief secured for Jamaica will be extended to all. Thus the delegation is working for our community ol Islands. They see before them an arduous, severe, and protracted struggle. They are sensible of their inability to successfully enter the contest unaided. They are calling upon us for support. They demand aid in order to enable them "to ' controvert the mass of ignorance and " misrepresentation," which impedes them in " their labours." Shall they have such aid ? Let the public of Antigua reply. Shall they and their righteous cause þÿ our causeþÿ be discarded ? Shall they be left to fight the battle alone? Shall we, who will share in their success, or participate in their defeat, abandon them heartlessly and ingloriously to the struggle? Or, shall

we not rather fly to their aid, and show, by an energetic movement, that there is life yet remaining in Antiguan veins; that, though wearied with adversity, she is not dispirited ; that her sons, though impoverished, are not degenerated? Surely some portion of the public zeal, conspicuous in her annals, is still inherited, and now is the moment for its demonstration. In so earnestly advocating this measure, we feel impelled by a sense of our public duty. A deep consciousness of our responsibility as a public organ, and an earnest desire to promote, to the ut-

most of our feeble powers, the interests of our adopted country, constrain us to be tli us urgent in summoning to its aid the talent and active influence of its public men. And although our mind, at the present moment, is distracted with difficulties pertaining to our business sphere, yet we could not permit even these in such a crisis to control and subdue us to ( silence. We trust the voice which we i thus raise, will not be discarded, but that gentlemen will, without delay, append their signatures to a requisition ' calling a Public Meeting, for the nomination of Delegates, the opening of subscriptions to the fund, and the consideration of such other matters as shall advance the object desired, and promote the resuscitation ofour naturally favoured and beautiful, but morally blighted, Island.

Buenos Aykes and its Prospects. þÿ The political and social position of Buenos Ayres is beginning to attract much more attention in this country than it was accustomed to have bestowed upon it previously to the last revolution, that relieved it from a tyrannical oppressor. Since the defeat of Rosas, and his expulsion from the country, the commercial interests, here and elsewhere, have been anxiously watching for the accounts received from thence, in order to ascertain the principles and character of the men who have carried out that great revolution, and to calculate what sort of a government they may expect to see erected over the ruins of that terrible despotism which had so long existed under the regime of the sanguinary Rosas. The intelligence, however, which reaches us from tliM remote part of South þÿ minute portions in mere dribbles þÿ America comes in very and so disconnected as to require a great deal of attention, care and industry to string these items together and arrive at an understanding of the course of events which have taken place in . that rich and distant country, and draw from them anything like an accurate opinion of its present position and prospects. Hitherto, Buenos Ayres and the immense adjacent provinces, watered by the numerous rivers of that region, have only been objects of interest or contemplation to a small portion of the mercantile community, and that principally in this city. The United States government also neglected, in the same manner, to cultivate

either commercial or political relations with those immense territories, leaving thereby a wider field for France and | every day more general ; but credit is claimed England to carry forward their intrigues in its affairs. It is to be hoped, however þÿ and we have seen some symptoms thereof in the new þÿmovements that the , government at Washington intends to pay much more attention in future to our commercial and politicalconnections with Buenos Ayres and the countries bordering the La Plata, than it has heretofore done. In furtherance of these ideas, pervading our government and animating the commercial interests connected with these countries, there has lately sprung up a great spirit of inquiry relative to the progress of important events there since the recent flight of Rosas, and the auspicious revolution that has taken foreign tobacco place in the internal government. According to all accounts, the symptoms are favorable, although our information on the subject is confused and fragmentary. The commercial interests will, of course, form the first matter of inquiry and settlement by the new government of Buenos Ayres and the neighboring provinces; but we have information that

ATI s. the social and religious condition of these countries has already occupied their attention, and received consideration of a favorable nature. The last accounts state that the religious intolerance, or exclusiveness, which has prevailed there for many years past, through the influence of the Catholic church, has been so far relaxed as to allow all foreigners and others to observe and celebrate t heir religious rites and ceremonies þÿ in their own way. This is a great boon an advance in the principles of civil and political rights, and it speaks favorably for the disposition and temper of the new government, and the men who have brought about the present state of public affairs. More time and better information are necessary, before a correct or full idea can be formed of the changes which the recent events in that country may work, j now and hereafter, on its condition in every point of view þÿ religious, social, and political. We shall watch with much interest the progress of affairs.

To the Editor of St. Croix Avis. Sir, I am glad to see that there is some one who sympathises with the difficulties of the position, in which the managers are placed, with respect to the election of members for the Colonial Assembly. Your advice is very good, so far as it goes, but for a poor fellow, who feels himself in a fix, and is little acquainted personally with the various qualities, or qualifications of the þÿ magnets, (I þÿ der you did not prefer the word mag- wonþÿnates ),who ought to figure at head quarters, I require some one to point out to me, and explain, who are the fittest persons. If it were a ploughing match, or a weeding match, or the best mode of planting canes, then, I should be able to make a selection amongst my fellow planters, that I have full confidence would do every justice to their appointment, and acquit themselves satisfactorily. But that I should be expected to know who are the best persons to cope with matters touching the general interests of the Island, is rather beyond the precincts of a þÿmanager s limited rane of life. And therefore it is that I seek to obtain some advice from you, as to those, to whom I ought to go for direction. I have no notion, in a free country like this, of being dictated to, merely because 1 am employed. Every man ought to exercise his own judgement, and I mean to do so. But I am at a loss whom to advise with. I own no Estate þÿ I have no stake in the country, and therefore have no personal interest þÿ except indeed, my em-
ployment, which I must confess is my all, as yet, in the world, and which I must also confess depends upon my employer,

3 T S Ui D AT 1 to a certain extent ; for if he is ruined, why, my þÿoccupation gone. s Suppose I go to town, and consult with the merchants, why, they may have some object in view, of which I am ignorant, and may recommend persons that they are sure will favor their peculiar interests. If I consult the lawyers, some of whom, I hear, are very desirous of being elected, they will probably take some trouble to prove that they, themselves are the fittest persons, because it is their interest to be impartial to all parties, and perhaps if I did not fall in with their views they might charge me for advice. I am, therefore, as it were, perforce thrown back upon my employer, and driven to ask his opinion. It is true I ought, perhaps, to have done that at first, out of courtesy, which I might have done, and still reserved my right of judgment. But I did not like the idea of dictation. And yet the more 1 reflect on it, the more convinced do I feel, that he is the only person with whom I could consult with propriety, or with a prospect of obtaining that information which would lead me to make a good selection. lie has property at stake, and that kind of property, which, as a whole, is the main interest of the colony þÿ without it the large merchants would have no existence, and their place þÿ would he filled up by petty shopkeepers the lawyers would have nothing left worth living here for þÿ the Government itself would have to be supported almost if not entirely from home þÿ and therefore 1 think he would be very careful to make

such a selection himself, as would tend to preserve or procure the prosperity of the chief and important interest of the colony þÿ and I, interested as I am by my profession, in the þÿplanters welfare, (thereby securing my own), do not think I can be far wrong in voting according to his views, or at any rate in seeking his advice. Now, Mr. Editor, I have just put down plainly, and as clearly as I can, my own thoughts on the subject, and hearing that some persons are very anxious to get themselves enrolled, as members of the Assembly, whose qualifications, through my ignorance, I am unable to judge of, and fearing that I might be meeting with some of them that might persuade me to a vote, that might turn out injudicious, 1 must beg you will favor me, at an early period, with your advice. Before closing 1 must remark how differently the affairs of the world are conducted here, to what I have read of in former days. The responsible offices of public trust were then filled by men of talent, and acknowledged ability; but who were so modest, in their own selfestimated qualifications, that they had to be sought for, and dragged forth from private life. How far the conduct of public aspirants of the present day correspond i leave to your own inference. A Country Voter. Our correspondent appears to be in great trouble, we see no difficulty in selecting proper persons for the Colonial Council and would advise him to be impartial.

Fearful Mortality on Board the Ship þÿ Lady þÿMontague. þÿ For some days past the Marine Department of the Board of Trade have been prosecuting an inquiry relative to a fearful case of mortality, involving no less than 274 deaths on board the British ship Lady Montague, on her voyage from China to Callao, with Chinese emigrants, 590 souls, including the crew, being on board when she left China. Sickness and fever seized the helpless crew a few days after her departure. The water and pro visions provided for the emigrants became putrid, as reported in the log. The sufferings of the poor people were of the most frightful description. Many committed suicide by jumping overboard; and by the time the ship put into Hobart Town, no fewer than 193 had perished. Some medical relief having been procured here the ship proceeded on her voyage, but by the time she reached her destination nearly 100 more had died. Only three out of a crew of thirty-six who went out with the ship have come home. The captain, Mr. Wells, had died on the outward voyage, when the command was taken by Mr. Smith, the chief officer, who, it is said, chartered the ship to carry emigrants contrary to the wishes of the owner. þÿ Ibid. -aiozt- IVihner and Smith's European Times, July 10, 1852.

There is now building on ihe Clyde, in die yard of Messrs Caird and Co., at Carts Dyke, an immense iron steam-ship, to be called the Atrato. of much greater capacity, and considerably larger, than that leviathan steamer the Great Britain; indeed, so large is the Atrato to he, that the fine steam-ship Arabia, of 2400 tons, whose launch in the Clyde the other day we last week noticed, might he put inside the new steamer, with a good deal of room to spare. The origin of the Atrato is somewhat romantic. Her builders, Messrs Caird and Co., having constructed the engines (of 850 horse- power) for the Demerara, which got jammed across the Severn, and had to he broken up in consequence of the straining she received, got on order from the West India steam-ship Company, to whom the Demerara bolonged, to build a vessel of iron instead of wood, to which the new engines might be adapted. They were permitted to modify the design of the hull so far as the length was concerned, although the retention of the original paddle-shafts compelled an adherence to the same breadth of beam at that line as the original vessel The result has been that the engineers submitted plans which were approved of, and are now being carried out in the building of the largest vessel ever afloat. The entire length of the keel is laid resting on Mocks. The enormous bar is in nine

8 T Q'M 0 2 'JL a t a pieces, joined by searfjoints, and firmly rivet- > ted together; it is the longest bar and the strongest bar we ever saw. The stern-post is in one piece, and so is the stem, which runs for about ten feet into the horizontal keel, The stern alone weighs GO cwt. Only one-half of the ribs or frames are as yet in place, and even with the long length of bare keel terminated by the stem standing up some 40 feet or more, the enormous dimensions of the vessel can hardly be appreciated. but they will be understood from the principal measurements of the Atrato. %aud those of the largest ship-of-war in the British service, the Windsor Castle, now on the stocks at Pembroke Dockyard, which is stated to tie þÿ tiie largest vessel in the þÿworld Their principal measurements are: þÿ THE ATRATO. The following is an account of the loss of the Isabella Watson, passenger ship to Port Philip, which sailed from Plymouth on the 3rd of December last, as given in an extract from a private letter: þÿ Melbourne, March 27. þÿ dear My , þÿ We are all safe and well, but have been shipwrecked off Point Nepean, at the entrance of Port Philip Heads. After a most pleasant and prosperous voyage we made Gape Utwiiv Light on Saturday night last, and considered our voyage as nearly ended. Sunday proved calm, and we stood along the land, as happy as people could well he; about four o'clock on Sunday afternoon we had a squall of wind, and came along at a fair rate, about nine knots an hour; between five and six we ran up our signal for a pilot and shortened sail. We were all on deck talking and chattjng when the ship struck on the point of the reef ; the helm was put about, and the necessary steps taken to bring the ship's head to sea again; she again struck, and apparently passed over the danger. 1 hurried A and the children into the cuddy, and then went and secured my moneybelt ; the ship struck again, and unfortunately, our helm was carried away; she broached to, and drifted broadside on the rocks; the masts were instantly cut away, and we expected every moment to be our last; the sea made a clean breach over us, and we prepared þÿ þÿA ourselves for the worst. 1 cut away 's flannel petticoat, and the other two ladies in the cuddy followed my example.
II C volunteered to take charge of the baby. My wife was mv care, and H clung close to me ; in the mean time the captain's gig was lowered, six persons de-

scended into it, viz , three sailors, one cabin passenger (a Mr. Gray), and two steerage passengers (a Mr. , and a little girl). It was the þÿcaptain i s ntention to send a rope on shore by this boat, but she drifted off. We saw them land on a tock, and the boat upset; they set her right again, and were saved ; ot the latter fact, however, we were not aware till Monday morning. Darkness increasing, with the force of the gale and heavy sea, it was deemed imprudent to attempt any further landing. However, on the earnest entreaties of some of the passengers, the captain was induced to have the life-boat lowered. The word was passed for the ladies and women who might wish to go in her. A was the first asked, but on her learning that 1 could not accompany her and the children (as 1, ot course, refused to leave while there were women willing to go in the boat), she positively tefused to leave me, stating she preferred being drowned with me to being saved and leaving me on board. Her courage and devotedness saved her life, as every soul but one iu the life-boat was drowned before our eyes. To resume. Seven women and one man got into the life-boat, the captain standing in the boat to steady Iter and using every exertion to place them in safely, when, dteadful to relate, she turned right over, and the whole were immersed iu lire water, and all, save one (Mrs. Patterson) drowned. The captain and crew, consisting of ten men and a passenger, hoisted out a boat, in which, after stowing away a bag of biscuits and a little water, they embarked, and in about fifteen minutes after the vessel was struck she sunk. The Screw Steamer "Tamauliþÿ This fine vessel, the pioneer of a line of screw steamers between this port and various places in the gulf of Mexico, arrived here from the Clyde last week, and, after receiving her cargo, sailed from hist, the for Wellington Dock þÿ her destination on Wednesday namely, St. Thomas, Jamaica, and Tampico. As there are several important features requisite in a vessel for which the " Tamaulipas" is intended, suitable to the trade a few general remarks as to her size and

lipas" has been built by Messrs. John Reid and Co., of Port Glasgow, (who have turned out some of the fastest screw-boats afloat,) expressly for the Tampico trade ; and her machinery, which is on the direct action principle, has been constructed by Messrs. J. and G. Thomson, of the Clyde Bank Foundry. She is a schooner-rigged vessel, of about 500 tons burthen, and of proportionate power. Her model, which is very beautiful, has been shaped with a view to speed, and she has consequently great length, sharpness fore and aft, and a light draft of water. The latter has been rendered necessary on account of the harbour of Tampico (which is the principal port of destination) having to be entered over a bar, so that vessels drawing much water could not cross without sometimes incurring considerable risk. On this account the rates of insurance on goods shipped by sailing vessels has always been very high; but as the "Tamaulipas" has been constructed so as to cross the bar at any time, with perfect safety, these charges are very materially reduced. The "Tamaulipas" is fitted with all the modern improvements, and every requisite that may be useful in the trade for which she is designed. She has a bullion chamber for the conveyance of specie, rendered doubly secure by containing a patent safe, which will hold a large amount of the precious metal. We have already mentioned her handsome model, which is set oft" to advantage by her hull being and rigging nicely adjusted, " man-of- relieved with painted ports, her spars

war fashion," and her funnel painted cream-colour, giving her altogether a light, ship-like, and "clipper" appearance. She has already proved herself a fast vessel, having accomplished eleven knots, under steam alone, on her passage from the Clyde to this port; and on Wednesday last, when goingout, deeply laden, she steamed from the Rock Light to the Bell Buoy in the face of a stiff north-west breeze, in a little under an hour. Her cabins are furnished in an elegant manner, and she has first-class accommodation for about twenty passengers, who will be under the care of Captain Robert Ewing, a gentleman who, from his long experience in steam navigation, is eminently fitted for " the com- mand of such a craft. The Tamaulipas" is the property of Messrs. Newal, Burt and Co., of this town, through whose enterprise the new line has been started.

Dcmerara : Prom this Colony we learn the painful intelligence of the death of the honorable Jeffery Hart Bent, Chief Justice of British Guiana, who expired calmly on -Tuesday, the 29th ultimo, in the 72nd year of his says "Mr. Bent was the oldest Judge in the West good þÿ old age. The Saint Lucia Palladium, of the 16th Indies. His first appointment was to the Bench of Grenada, and the Grenadines. An Act of the Legislature of those Islands, of November 15, 1820, shows that the appointment must /lave been made upwards of thirty years ago. It says þÿ "'Whereas nothing can tend more effectually to preserve the dignity of our courts of justice than that the office of chief justice should be filled by a man of should be enabled properly to support and maintain integrity, legal knowledge, and ability, and that the he dignity as well as independence of that high important situation ; and whereas the fees appertaining thereto are inadequate to these purposes ; be it there- fore enacted,' " &c , '"that there shall be levied and raised, yearly, within this government, and paid to lic treasurer of the same, as long as the Jeffery Hart Bent, Esquire, or to his order, said by the pub- Jeft'ery Hart Bent shall continue to fill and discharge the du-

ties of the office of chief justice of these islands, a clear yearly sum or salary of £2,500 of current " money, to commence from the 16th of October last.' " About twelve years after this provision, Mr. Bent was removed to the office of an assistant-judge in the island of Trinidad, which he occupied for a short time, and in the early part of 1833 was appointed chief justice of St. Lucia. From personal experience and observation, the writer of these lines bears willing testimony, without any disparagement to the lamented gentleman's learned predecessors and successors, that a more enlightened, impartial and upright judge never sat upon the bench in either of those islands. " In the circumstances of the colony," observes Mr. Breen, in his History of St. Lucia, " a better selection could not have been made; nor indeed could there have been found, throughout the wide range of our West Indian possessions, a gentleman better qualified for the judicial office under any circumstances. Upright, impartial, and single-minded, in Mr. Bent were happily blended, in a high degree, the ability and tact of the sound constitutional lawyers, and that spirit of independence so eminently characteristic of the true English Judge. Having spent many years in the exercise of various judicial functions in New ijoutli Wales, his experience in both hemispheres was only surpassed by his integrity, and that was as much above suspicion as it was beyond the reach of slander. Punctilious to the extent

to which punctiliousness is a virtue in the judicial character, and yet active to a degree almost incompatible with his delicate state of health, he infused into the different offices connected with the courts a taste for regularity and order which continues to be productive of the most beneficial results even to this day." " From St. Lucia, Mr. Bent was, in 1836, promoted to the more lucrative Judgeship of British Guiana, where, after sixteen years' service, he expired on the 29th ultimo." The St. Lucia Palladium publishes the subjoined from Martinique : "On the celebration of the Fete Dieu, on Sunday, at Martinique, the flag-ship hoisted an English Ensign under the French ; the English Consul, Mr. Law- þÿ less þÿ remonstrated ; when the flags were reversed, the English being put above the French, but with the union downwards; a second remonstrance was the consequence, when the matter was put right The flag man was sent to "durance vile," and an order issued that the English Flag should be kept flying the whole of the follow ing day." " We have received the following from J. Lawless, Esq., British Consul at Martinique, in rectification of a misstatement copied into The Palladium of the 2nd inst. from a Dominica paper : þÿ St. Pierre, Martinique, 9th July, 1853. My dear Sir, þÿ In your Palladium of the 2nd inst., you published an article, extracted from a Dominica paper, the untruth of which obliges me, although unwillingly, to write on the subject. It is not true that' on the celebration of the Fete Dieu in St. Pierre, the flag-ship, or even a merchantship, hoisted an English ensign under the French. It was done by the master of one of the Island droghers who had decorated his vessel with flags ; and I was at first w illing to believe that he had done so through ignorance, as represented, since the flag was struck as soon as 1 made a verbal remonstrance on the subject. Had there been a man-of-warof any kind in the harbour, I am convinced that the circumstance would not have

occurred at all. However, the flag having been again hoisted about an hour afterwards- union down þÿ 1 could no longer suffer ignorance, or even intoxication, to be offered in excuse ; and therefore lodged an official remonstrance, winch was immediately and courteously attended to. Be pleased to insert the foregoing rectification in your next Palladium ; and believe me to be, My dear Sir, Faithful yours, J. LAWLESS. Charles Wells, Esq , Editor of The Palladium, St. Lucia." The same journal gives us the following account of the state of affairs in Guadeloupe : Guadeloupe. þÿ The advent of M. Charles Dain, a Red Republican Socialist, recently appointed by Louis Napoleon to office in the Appeal Court of Guadeloupe, and who arrived from France by the second June packet, had been the cause of great excitement and of new disorders in that colony. On the arrival of the steamer at Basseterre on the morning of the 5th inst., M. Itusson, Director of the interior, and M. Valine, inspector-general of the police, went on board and advised M. Dain not to go ashore at the usual landing place, but disregarding this advice, he landed, and, in

by the assembled multitude. He had to move under despite of all that the police and gendarmerie could do, he was immediately surrounded, hooted, and menace the protection of the police; yet that did not "save him from being the object of a general and most boisterous charivari until his departure at night for the country. Thirtv young gentlemen of the best families were arrested and imprisoned, for the part they took in the demonstration. On the following day Governor Aubry- Bailleul issued a proclamation, threatening the severest punishment should the street tumults be renewed. Ou the 7th, an escort of 12 gendarmes had to attend the obnoxious functionary to the government-house to pay his official visit. Notwithstanding all this display of force, fresh tumults arose, and numerous arrests had again to be made. The manifestation then assumed a more serious character, and passed from the streets into the constituted institutions. The members of the municipal council of Basseterre, with the honorable M. Laurichesse at their head, with the single exception of a brother in-law of M. Dain, simultaneously threw up their place, avowing the manifestation which hud takeu pace in the town as the true expression of the feeling of the country, and in which the council entirely concurred. The members of the bar of Basseterre assembled and solemnly refused to plead before the Court a long as M. Dain continued one of its members. Even the privy council gave in its resignations, considering

the appearance of M. Dain in the administration of the colony to be a great evil, and not wishing to share in the responsibility of the dangers which might be the consequence of those extreme measures of which he would be the leading and deplorable cause. On the news reaching l'ointe a l'itre, on the 9th, the murmur was general. The municipal council, the chambers of commerce, and officers of the militia, gave in their resignation en masse, giving as their reasons that it was impossible for them to continue in office while they should find themselves exposed to mingle with the confidant ol Seiiecal. The same feeling indignation and of disgust had spread over the whole colony."

The French and British West Indies. þÿ So much had been said of the superior civilization of the French West Indian islands over the British that I was curious to see the difference and to trace its cause. The houses, both in town and country are much on a par, taking into, consideration, of course, the slight difference between English neatness and French show and the domestic usages of the two countries; but, in the inhabitants, there is a great difference, mostly, I regret to say, in favour of the French, who are all amenity of manner, full of different from the course the bienseance of humanity, pleasingly- vulgarity and which but too often characterizes the English out here. This arises from the difference of rank and education in the two parties ; the propria /aires being generally men of good families who have received their education at some French university, and their patrimonies from their great grandfathers; whilst, among the English, the true tropical squire absolutely is extinct, and bis place is usurped by some thriving tradesman, a vulgar fellow, who, battening, on the liberal expenditure of his ci-devant customer, has mortgaged himself into possession; and then, with his hat on one side and his arms akimbo, set up for a planter. This dignity he shares with Scotch ploughmen, who come out of some sheiling, in the Highlands, and have skinned every flint, until they have bought the estate of their former master over his head. With the shopkeepers it is somewhat different.

The French shopkeeper adopts some tropical city as bis home, and he at once marries and settles himself down as a stone of the soil, intending his creole family to be his successors ; whilst the English shopkeeper, on the contrary, a tradesman in origin, feelings, and habits, comes out hereto get as much as he can and then return home an independant man. The result of all this is that the Frenchman seeks to improve all around him, to supply, as lie best may, pleasures which in Europe had become habits, and hence the theatres, the cafeet, the billiard tables, &c. that are met with in the French islands. The Englishman does as little as possible for his island, careless as to what becomes of it the moment after his departure, his only ties being halfa-dozen illegitimate children, for whom he does little, and cares less. þÿ Day's Five Years' Residence in the West Indies.

The "AVIS." Christiansted, Friday the 13th of August 1852. The St. Thomas Times of the 4th instant gives a recapitulation of the Voters respectively in these Islands, and in reference thereto remarks: "that St. Croix with 307 votes, returns eight members to the Council ; that St. Thomas, with 347 votes, returns six members ; that St. Johns, with 14 votes, returns two members," from which statement it would appear the conclusion is drawn, that a disproportionate number of members is returned for St. Thomas. When we, however, compare the population of this Island with that of St. Thomas, a far different view of the matter is obtained, and it becomes then quite clear and evident, that St. Croix returns only a number of members in proportion to its population, as is " justly his correspondent A" in observed by our article, which appears in this number. The same paper states: "The subject, it is plain to be seen, admits of ample prophecy and prognostication as to ultimate results, but we forbear for the present to dilate on any of them, preferring to leave the question to the wisdom of certain gentlemen who have lately been writing long letters to a neighbouring newspaper, purporting to show bow competent they are to render a critical review of the affairs of Colonies, and of 'Colonial Laws.'" Surely the people of St. Thomas can have nothing to fear from the opinions expressed by these gentlemen; for we notice nothing impartial or narrow-minded in their writings; but should rather think that they have evinced pure and uninteresting mo-

tives, which characterize good citizens. The steamer " Trent," which arrived at St. Thomas on the 31st of last month, has, we learn, brought intelligence from Chagres, that the Cholera and Yellow Fever prevail there to a fearful extent. There were several cases on board the steamer, two of which proved fatal þÿ one passenger and one of the crew died on the passage from Chagres to St. Thomas. It appears that the unhealthiness of Chagres and its vicinity, is owing chiefly to its locality and peculiar climate, and although its communication with foreign countries is very great, it has not come to our knowledge that the infection has spread to any of these places. There is scarcely any doubt but that many who seek employment there will fall victims to the ravages of these dreadful diseases ; and experience teaches, that strangers not inured to the climate of a new place of residence, and not taking the necessary precautions, are more liable to diseases, which in nine cases out of ten prove mortal. We hear that quarantine measures are about being taken in St. Thomas, with regard to the stcamersarrivingthere fromChagres, which, to judge from what we have already stated, may not be absolutely necessary. This intelligence will, no doubt, materially lessen the disposition, evinced of late in some of the British West India Islands, to emigrate thither in search of more lucrative employment, which circumstance, at a certain time, also induced many of our countrymen to try

For the St. Croix Avis. The " St. Thotme Tidende" of the 4th inst. has an article containing some remarks in regard to the number of voters for the three Islands, St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. Johns, compared with the number of members to be chosen, for each of these Islands, for the Colonial Assembly, showing that while St. Croix and St. Johns þÿ "both agricultural districts" þÿ with 321 voters return ten members, St. Thomas þÿ " principally commercial" þÿ returns only six members. This is certainly disproportionate, if the number of qualified voters in each of the Islands be taken as the standard for the comparison, and if it should be the paramount duty of the members in the Assembly to represent the interest of classes or the particular interest only of the Island for which he is returned, this disproportion would certainly tell against St. Thomas. But this appears to be rather a narrow view of the duty devolving on the Colonial Members and is not justified either by the words or the spirit of the Colonial Law. The duty of the members must certainly be to represent and defend the rights and interests of all the inhabitants of the Danish Weslindia Islands without regard to professions, classes or colour, and the standard for the comparison will then be the number of inhabitants in each Island and not the number of individuals possessing franchise right. Thus compared it will be seen, that St. Thomas, so far from being in the minority in the representation, does in proportion return more members

to the Colonial Assembly than St. Croix and St. Johns together. The census of 1850 shows the number of inhabitants in St. Croix to be 23,720; in St. Thomas 13,060 and in St. Johns 2,228. Thus St. Croix and St. Johns together only return one member for 2595 inhabitants, whereas St. Thomas alone returns one for 2278 inhabitants. A.

Illustrated London News, July 10, 1852. FRAN! C E. The session of the French Senate was closed on Monday; Marshal (the ex- King) Jerome Bonaparte presided on the occasion. Several bills which had been referred to the Senate for consideration having been disposed of, the President of the Senate rose and pronounced a

closing address, which was received with numerous marks of sympathy and approbation. Count X. de Casabianca, the the Minister of State, was then introduced, and read the proclamation declaring the Senate to be closed. The senators at once separated. Rumours were afloat on Tuesday in Paris that a change of Ministry was about to take place, when M. Morny, it was thought, would enter the Cabinet. The hot weather has brought with it hydrophobia. Several persons in the streets of Paris have been bitten by dogs labouring under that disease ; and one lady, who had been so attacked, ran about the streets on Monday last, attempting to bite every person that came i in her way, and shortly afterwards died. On Tuesday a child was taken to one of the hospitals, having been almost half devoured by one of these rabid animals. The Moniteur announces, in a communicated note, that the President, having been informed of the intention to give banquets in his honour during his approaching tour in#the departments, has resolved not to accept any, however touched he is by these kind attentions. Monseigneur Pallegoix, member of the Congregation of Foreign Missions, has arrived in France from Siain. lie is charged by the King of Siam with a friendly mission to the President of the Republic, and is about to bring out a dictionary in Latin Siamese. His present title is Bishop of Mallos, but he has for some time been acting as Bishop of Siam, and as the prelate of that see died recently, it is supposed that he will be

named his successor. When M. Pallegoix first went to Siam there were only 1500 Roman Catholics, and there are now upwards of 7000. The number of priests composing bis mission is fifteen, seven of them being natives. The reports from the provinces give the most favorable accounts of the state of the crops. Two Arabs, imprisoned in the fort of St. Louis, atCette, had a violent quarrel a few days since, which resulted in one of them plunging his knife into the stomach of his opponent, from which the wounded man shortly afterwards died.

The Emperor of Russia has again taken a sudden journey to Berlin. He reached the 1'russian capital on ihe 10th instant. In the Paris correspondence of one of the best informed London journals we perceive that u report was current that the Czar immediately on his arrival at Berlin was seized with a fit of apoplexy, and was dangerously indisposed. The rumour has not been since eonfnmed, but considering the precautions invariably taken in similar cases to keep the knowledge of such calamities from the public, its nonconformation bv no means proves that there is no foundation for the report. However such an important event cannot be kept secret many days in a foreign capital We need not dwell upon the important political consequences .which would result from the Czars demise at this juncture. He is playing the most important part of any prince in Europe. True to the policy of the imperial cabinet, he is the arbiter and protector of all Germany, lie throws a shield over Belgium, encourages Bavaria, and holds out a hand to the States of the Church in Italy and Naples He is the only barrier against Louis Napoleon's agression Whilst England has her hands tied and fears to move, the Czar has organized an alliance to secure the peace of Europe, by keeping Louis Napoleon in check within the limits of France, and we fear that the removal of the Czar would he attended by the most serious consequences to all Europe. The Danish Soldier. þÿ The Danish soldier appears to suitthe people of Sleswick better than their volunteer liberators did, although engaged in the same cause. " Schleswig-Ilolstein" friends were of a They complain that their very unaccommodating character, and were always craving more and better food, lodging, and attendance than the peasants could give, and would not help at all at any farm-work. The carousing, visiting, gossiping, antl never-ending singing, night and day, did not at all suit the quiet, sedate, routine of life of the peasants of llolstein and Sleswick. The southern Germans are a lively, enthusiastic, life-enjoying people compared to the northern people of the same race. They are as different in temperament, character, and habits, as the French and English. After the first burst of enthusiasm was over, the men who filled the ranks of the free corps, ranting, jovial students, artists, and persons of higher station, and with higher and more troublesome, wants and demands than the ordinary soldier, were by no means welcome inmates in the peasant's house. The Danish soldier is a quiet, hardworking man, who goes about the peasant's farm-yard like one of his own farm servants, puts up with the same fare and lodging, looks after the cattle, feeds the pigs, and makes himself useful. He is a husbandman under arms, and in all his tastes he is agricultural as well as military. An interesting anecdote is told of this mixture of character. At the siege of Frederickstadt, while thirty-

two pieces of heavy artillery were pouring shot and shells incessantly into a little country town, which was deserted by the inhabitants and on fire, on all sides, the great subject of conversation and sympathy among the Danish soldiers of the little garrison was not their own killed or wounded, but the cattle, the poor cattle left in the burning house. One soldier was observed to steal across the street while it was swept by the enemy's fire, and was found by his officer coolly dealing out provender to the deserted and hungry cattle of his landlord. He could not withstand their bellowing for food. þÿ Laing's Denmark and the Duchies.

The Operative Classes in Copenhagen. The confidence reposed by the public authorities of Copenhagen in the orderly conduct of the people is well responded to by the people. The young trees and shrubs, the scats and monuments in the parks and public walks, require no protection but the good feeling of the public. The streets are but poorly lighted, gas is not jet introduced, and the police is an invisible force ; yet one may walk at all hours through this town without seeing one disorderly person, a man in liquor unable to take care of himself, or a female street-walker. Every one appears to have a home and bed of some kind, and the houseless are unknown as a class. One great cause of the general well-being and orderly conduct of the operative body in Copenhagen, even in its lowest employments, is, that no attraction is offered by chance-work in any regular trade or occupation for the artizan or workingman to leave his own place and resort to the capital. Such chance-work for strangers can rarely occur in the trades under the incorporation system, and the stranger must be known and recommended by the masters of his ciaft in the place he comes from. There is no such influx, as in our large towns, of operatives in every trade, who, coming from the country to better their condition, are bv far too numerous for the demand, must take work at lower and lower wages to keep themselves from starving, and who reduce their fellow craftsmen and themselves to equal misery. Employment is more
fixed and stationary for the employed and for

3 JN 0 D t 31 A T I 3 the employers. There is no foreign trade or home consumption to occasion great and sudden activity and expansion in inauulactuies, and equally great and sudden siagnuiion and collapse. The home market is of known and limited extent ; each manulactu er knows how much his own circle of customers require of his goods, and it is only by slow degrees that he can extend his circle and employ more hands. The greatest body of the operative class of Copenhagen consists ol workmen employed by government about the dock-yard These are lodged in small, neat houses, one siory high, in regular airy streets, which government build for lodging its workmen and seamen not afloat. The comfort and cleanliness of these dwellings appear to have given a kind of standard of requirements to workmen in private employment, and a standard also of conduct. Drunkenness and drinking are two vices which have disappeared from the Danish character. þÿ Laing's Denmaik and the Duchies.

The Drama in Copenhagen. þÿ 1 was very much struck in Copenhagen with the good taste shown in ail minor matters connected with the drama, such taste as I must acknowledge I have never seen surpassed anywhere. 1 believe " some people" might learn a great deal by a visit to Copenhagen, and a minute inspection of these matters. In costumes, decorations, and all the endless concerns not authoritatively laid down by a dramatic vvriter in his play, the people in office about the Theatre-Royal seem, by a happy instinct, to light upon just the right and proper tiring. There is a completeness, a suitableness, an external unity that gives the feeling of a perfect piece of art to every evening's performance. It is invaluable to have all minor matters in right trim. One peculiarity about which there might be divers opinions is the disposal oflight. During every performance the body of the house is darkened, the great chandelier in the centre being drawn up into the roof, and all the light is upon the stage. The effect, in my opinion, is admirable ; but, as I said, there may be different views of the matter. The Danes are enthusiastic playgoers; and the Theatre in Denmark is a more perfectly unobjectionable institution than it is in some countries of Europe. It is so far from having the most distant tendency towards demoralization, that it is rather looked upon as an important agent in the cultivation and improvement of the people. And it is so looked upon by the best and most en-

lightened of Denmark's sons, among others by the most influential evangelical clergy. As it exits in Denmark it is a very valuable institution. Unfortunately, it is only too difficult for other nations to copy the best points in the constitution of the Danish theatre, for such must rather grow up from within. One thing I may mention is, the general estimable character of the performers employed at the Copenhagen theatre. Morality is as strictly demanded in actors and actresses as in any other people. The reverse of morality would involve immediate dismissal. Hence the position which members of this body generally assume in Danish society. þÿ Hamilton's Sixteen Months in the Danish Isles.

Adulterated Cayenne Pepper. þÿ The Lancet gives the following result of an analysis of 28 samples of Cayenne " pepper That out ofthe 28 samples of Cayenne obtained at different þÿshops: pepper subjected to analysis, 24 were adulterated ; that out of the above number four only were genuine; that out of the 24 adulterated samples, 22 contained mineral colouring matter; that red lead, often in large and poisonous quantities, was present in 13 samples; that Venetian red, red ochre, brick dust, or some other analogous ferruginous earths, were contained in seven samples; that cinnabar, Vermillion, or sulphuret of mercury, was detected in one sample; that 6 of the samples consisted of a mixture of ground rice, turmetic, and Cayenne, coloured with either red lead or a red ferruginous earth; that six samples contained large quantities of stilt, sometimes alone, but more frequently combined with rice and a red ferruginous earth or with red lead ; that one ofthe samples was adulterated with a large quantity of the husk of white mustard seed ; that two contained rice only, coloured with red lead or a ferruginous earth. As is well known, red lead and vermillion, or sulphuret of mercury, are highly deleterious substances, both being characterised by the very peculiar circumstances tjiat they are not, like the majority of other compounds, when received into the system, at once eliminated therefrom, but remain in the body for a considerable time, gradually accumulating, until tit length they occasion

the peculiar symptoms which distinguish their presence in large amount. Thus, however small the dose taken from day to day, the constitution is yet liable, by the repetition ofthe dose, to he at length brought under the influence of the poison, and to become seriously affected. But Ihe quantity of red lead and mercury introduced into the system in adulterated cayenne pepper is by no means inconsiderable, since it commonly forms a large portion ofthe article. Some idea of the amount of these substances frequently present may he formed from Ihe tact that in a pinch ofcayenne, moistened and diffused over a white plate, or a piece of glass, they may he distinctly seen by the eye alone. What punishment, we would now inquire, ought, to he inflicted on the parties guilty of the crime of mixing these dclerious substances with articles of diet ? The case made out, we submit, is one which, for the sake of the public health, strongly demands the interposition of t lie Legislature. The man who steals one's purse commits a less crime then he who, by tricking our food, robs us of health. In a recent leading article we pointed out the fact that the law, in its present state, actually offers a remedy, which if, carried into effect, would to some extent meet the present case. Parties guilty of vending adulterated articles of food may be proceeded against for the recovery of the amount paid for them. We trust that some spirited individuals, having the welfare of the public at heart, will

The Observer, July 18, 1852. The Australian Gold Regions. VICTORIA. The Victoria gold fields still engross the chief attention of fortune-hunters, and really the out-movings appear to be immense. In five months, say from October, 1851, to the beginning of March, 1852, the Victoria diggings yielded the enormous amount of 653,270 ounces of gold, which is valued at £2,319,108 10s., or nearly 10,000,000 dollars. The Melbourne journals contain numerous instances of outrages committed on life and property at the mines, and we need hardly wonder at such a state of things, as thousands of pounds are passing daily in cash and gold, and thousands more in stores. The absence of rain was severely felt, and in most places the miners were unable to work owing to the drought. The miners complained loudly of the exaction of the monthly license fee when they were unable to work. A correspondent, writing from Mount Alexander, April 4, notices the improvements in progress, and the measures being adopted to introduce wholesome municipal regulations. The road through the diggings is progressing: the logs are cleared out of the line, banks cut away to form a level, holes filled up, many of the latter being fifteen feet deep, and merely filled up with loose earth. During the winter these holes will form a bog, out of which it will puzzle the unfortunate to get. The writer then goes on to remark, A material clrnnge has taken place " on the roads. Last week nil were wending their way to Melbourne, now the tide has turned, and thousands are coming to the diggings, trusting that rain will

fall shortly, and they will then be on the ground for work." The Emigration Movement. A number of clerks in the General Post Office and in the Tithe Office, Somerset House, have resigned their situations to proceed to Australia. Nine young men belonging to Blandford, in Dorsetshire, embarked at Gravesend on Thursday for the gold diggings at Port Philip. These young men could all have done well in this country. Last week a ship called the Exact sailed from Jersey, laden with emigrants from that island for Port Philip. fVilmer and Smith's European Times, August 16, 1852. Denmark and (lie Duchies. In the sitting of the German Diet on the 29th of July the propositions submitted by Austria and Prussia relative to the pacification of Holstein, as well as to the proclamation of the King of Denmark of the 28th of January, 1852, were adopted by the striking majority of 15 against 2. The propositions, which had been concerted beforehand with Denmark, were accepted purely and simply, without the slightest attempt at modification. Thus the differences between Denmark and the Germanic Confederation are definitively settled and arranged.

FRANCE. The Cabinet is now definitely constituted as follows : þÿ State, Fould ; Finance, Dineau; Public Works, Magne ; Foreign Affairs, Drouyn de Lhuys; Marine, Ducos; Justice, Ahhatucci; Instruction, Fortoul ; Interior, Persigny ; War, St. Arnaud ; Police, Maupas. Of these ten Ministers the first half represent the administrative capacity and sober views of the Cabinet. In the second half are to be found the Ministers of the coup d'etat, and the old party of the Elysee. It is now known that the destination of the French fleet is Tripoli, where a disputehas occurred between the French consul, M. Pelissier, and the Regency. It is said that the fleet has orders to bombard Tripoli, unless full satisfaction is given to the French Government. The opening of the Exhibition of the Works of the French and Foreign Artists for next year, is announced by the Minister of the Interior for March 15. On the 14th of August will come on the trial of Fradeaux, the wretch who has assassinated four wives in succession. The last of these murders, which has led to the detection of the rest, was only discovered the other day by a flower girl, whom lie wanted to replace his victim. The second " Feast of Eagles" is to be celebrated in Paris, with great pomp, on the 15th instant. The ceremony will be preceded by a high mass, which will be performed by the Archbishop of Paris, assisted by the whole of the clergy. The President will then proceed to the place appointed for the distribution of the eagles to the National Guard

of France, deputations from which are expected from the departments. The Place de la Concorde will be brilliantly illuminated, as also the whole line extending thence to the Barriere de I' Etoile, and on the summit of the triumphal arch will appear in gas an immense eagle, with wings spreading out sixty feet in extent. POKTIikAL. Our accounts from Lisbon are up to the 29th ult. Nothing of importance has been transacted in the Chamber of Peers since our last communication. The Lower House, however, had been busily engaged for some three weeks in disposing of the various acts of the dictatorship, all of which had been approved, with the exception of that about the capitalisation of government arrears, so often referred to in our notices of late. On this measure the government sustained a signal defeat in a majority of 80 to 38 ; nor did various amendments and propositions meet with a better reception. We may instance that of the Finance Committee, which was lost by 71 to 47. The o/ily alternative then left to the ministers was a resignation. They accordingly proceeded to the Palace to restore their portfolios, which, upon deliberation, were not accepted, her Majesty determining rather to dissolve the Chamber of Deputies. This was forthwith done, and the Cortes closed. The elections were to take place immediately, preceded, however, we are informed by a new electoral decree. The announcement of the dissolution of the Chamber caused no agitation in the city ; all was going on as usual. þÿ Ibid.

Another Fire at Sea. A passenger by the Severn gives the following account of a fire, which broke out in that vessel on her homeward voyage, and which well nigh led to a catastrophe as appalling as the late occurrence with the Amazon: The Severn left Madeira at about 6 p. m. of Thursday, the 5th inst., with upwards of 1 10 passengers, or, including the crew, with more than 200 souls on board. At between 1 and 2 o'clock of the following S iturday morning, the 7th, I was awoke by tny child, who slept in a cradle in my cabin, crying. While

trying to get him to sleep I suspected I smelt smoke. I opened a small window which looks down into the saloon, when I at once discovered the body of the ship filling fast with smoke, rising from the saloon cabin below, where, strange to say, numbers were sleeping totally unconscious of their danger. I at once gave the alarm by crying " Fire on board !" Mr. Rooker, who occupied an adjoining berth, was the first to hear me, when he, undressed as he was, at once rushed upon deck to give notice to the officer of the watch. Admiral Grenfell, who slept in another adjoining berth, immediately called Captain Chapman, and accompanied him below to whence the smoke proceeded. By this time all the passengers in the after part of the ship had heard the confusion, and were rushing upon deck half dressed, the body of the vessel filling fast with smoke. The captain, officers, and crew deserve the greatest credit for their coolness and promptitude of action throughout. Mr. Strutt, the chief officer, went below, and at the imminent risk of his own life from suffocation, descended to where the fire I was burning, and by his exertions was | mainly instrumental in saving the ship and lives of all on board. Mr. Leeds, the second officer, was employed in seeing an ample supply of water sent below, while Mr. Richards, the third officer, who remained in charge of the deck, sawthat the boats were ready to be lowered in case of necessity; but as they were insufficient to have held the whole of the

passengers and crew, it is to be supposed much loss of life would have ensued had they been called into requisition. In less than half an hour the fire was entirely got under, and by degrees the passengers became reassured. It has not been possible to discover how the fire originated. It commenced at and was confined to the after part of the ship, below the saloon, where the water tanks are kept ; this space is divided by a bulkhead from that allotted to the wine, spirits, and other stores for passengers use. It is suspected that one of the servants, a short time previous to the fire breaking out, must have gone down with the view of stealingsomething i to drink, when the accident may haVe occured. Upon the tanks were the remains of some beer casks, and some straw which had burnt, the side of the ship had taken fire, and it had worked its way along to the bulkhead, which in j less than two minutes more would have burnt so far as to communicate with the adjoining storeroom, where, in addition to wine, &,c., there was an abundance of straw, the ends of some of which were beginning to show the effects of fire. In such case there would have been little chance of saving the ship; the deck above, and the berths, all of pine, would have burnt too readily; moreover, the smoke would then have prevented any one approaching the spot. Upon first removing the grating leading to the tanks the fire was plainly seen burning, and only after a supply of water had been procured was it possible to go

below. This, however, was at hand, and very fortunately, also, Mr. Strutt. the first officer, who led the way, and risked his life to save the ship. Captain Chapman had the misfortune to fall twice while superintending below. He was very much hurt, broke one of his ribs, and has been suffering much since. þÿ Ibid.

GI1ADKLOIPE. Points Pitre, 27th July 1852. The Agricultural Society of Guadeloupe, in its sitting of Saturday last, adopted the following Petition relntive to a termination of the Colonial Indemnity. We publish it with the |>erinission of the Society : to mgr; the prince president of the þÿrepublic Monseigneur. The Agricultural Society of Guadeloupe, recently organized in Point Pitre, deem it its duty to devote its lirst deliberations on those questions of greatest vitality for the Colonies. Among the number there is to be found one which it asks of you the permission to submit to your exalted wisdom, the insufficiency "f the indemnity allotted to the colonists dispossessed of their ancient slaves. The abolition of slavery being an inevitable and positive fact ; as early as 1830 the Government appointed a Committee of Investigation, of which the Duke de Broglie was the Chairman, and whose enlightened and conscientious Report produced so great a sensation in 1813. But it would have required to avert the disastrous consequences of emancipation that it had been undertaken by a powerful and regular Government, amidst a tranquil slate of the public mind, and the prosperous condition of the metropolis. It has been effected in one day, during a tempe-t, and immediately after a revolution. From thence have arisen all those evils which the colonies (particularly Guadeloupe) have had to encounter, anarchy, abandonment of labor, and misery. The colonies, Prince, have not only experienced the

loss of their slaves : Emancipation has caused to rural property so extensive a depreciation that it cannot be disposed of to-day but at a fifth part of their former value. The sales either private or at public auction offer daily, the lamentable evidences of the truth adduced. Such depreciation is evidently the result of the difficulty of pursuing the works of cultivation, the absence of capital or means to provide for all the requirements of agriculture. If the indemnity had been in the first instance sufficient, if it had been paid at the time the emancipation was decreed, there is no doubt that this great social measure would have been accomplished without a shock, and without disturbance : but it was only in 1849, when about to separate, that the legislative Assembly voted that insignificant indemnity which gives to Guadeloupe 496 francs 28 c. (or each Slave, whilst the Committee, ol which the Duke de Broglie was the head, stipulated the amount at 1,200 frs. Nevertheless, adinist the unfortunate situation awarded to them, the proprietors have not been discouraged.

JN G ATI 3 They have multiplied their efforts, imposing on themselves all the sacrifices imaginable þÿ all lha. was possible to uphold labor, and to afford all the facility to the transformation about to take place. To-day, their means are exhausted ; the settlement of the indemnity can alone preserve them f-orn being totally ruined. « The settlement of that indemnity, which would be equally advantageous to the labourers as wel. as to the proprietors, and also the commerce of France, the Society of Agriculture, and with it the Inhabitants of Guadeloupe look for and expect from the considerate justice of your enlightened and amending Government. We ha\'e the honor to be, " Monseigneur," With a profound respect, Your most humble and most obdt. arrets., (Signed) E. REISET, President. P. CLARET, i Vice Presi- T. L'HERMINIER, dents. Harper's Magazine. There was an amusing account given some twenty years ago in an English periodical, of a footman to a gentleman in a provincial town (which wascrowded with strangers onsome week of rejoicing, or of some convention or other), being sent, as a favor, to cut the hair of a friend of his master's, who had " put up" at a neighboring inn. He had tried to shave a person once before, on an emergency, and cut his own thumb haltoft' through his cheek. His experience in hair-cutting was not much more fortunate; hut let him tell his own story: " The first sight of my new ' patient' set my nerves dancing in all directions. He was a large, tall, brawny, red-hot Irishman, with a head of hair bright orange, and curly as the wool of a negro. "'Cut my hair!' he said, in a voice like the grating of wagon-wheels ; 'and, you spalpeen, be handy wid ye, for it's these twenty-four hours that I'm after waiting for ye.' " The stranger's hair was stiff as wire ; of an inveterate tight round curl; and bushy to absolute frightfulness from excess of luxuriant growth. He had started from London with it rather too long; worn it uncombed on a three months' journey through Wales; and was waiting until he could arrive at some town where he could have it cut in the fashion. '" Cut my Jiair! I say, you devil's baby;' said the jollicking, roystering Irishman, imbibing at the same time a large draught from a tumbler of bramly-and-water, which he was consuming while he dressed, and recommencing, in a horrible

voice, to sing 'The Lads of Shillelagh,' a measure which my entrance had for a moment interrupted. " I obeyed, hut with a trembling hand. The very first sight of his head had discomposed all my faculties. I plunged into the operation of adjusting it as into a voyage over sea, without rudder or compass. I cut a hit here and a hit there, taking off very little at a time, for fear of losing my way; but the detestable round curl, rolling itself up at the very moment 1 let go the end, defeated every hope, every chance of regularity. " ' Thin the rest /' blasphemed the sufferer, ' for I'll not wait. Thin it, and leave it.' "This command put the finishing stroke to my perplexity. 'Thinning' was a process entirely beyond my skill ; but- a fresh execration, interrupting, ' The Lads of Shillelagh,' left me no longer any power of thought. I had seen the business of 'thinning' performed, although I did not at all comprehend it. I knew that the scissors were to he run through the hair from one side to another with a sort of snip þÿ snip þÿ snip, þÿ all the way, so I dashed on ; snip þÿ snip þÿ through the close, round, red snip curls, quite surprised at my own dexterity, for about a minute ajul a half; and then, taking up my comb, to collect the

proceeds of the operation, more than three-fourths of the man's hair came off in my hands! Wh at followed I have never exactly been clear in remembering. I think my victim must have felt the sudden chill occasioned by the departure of the thick-set hedge that constituted his head-gear. At all events, he put his hand to his head, and motioned as if he ' did address himself to rise.' I made a rush for the door, muttering something about being obliged to 'go for the heating-irons;' but as I turned round for a parting glance 'at that misguided man,' I saw discovery in his eye. Indeed, I see him in my mind's eye even now, with a countenance more in amazement than in anger, standing paralyzed, beside the chair upon which he had been sitting, and rubbing his head with the left hand, as if doubting whether his right hand had not misinformed him ; but at the moment when the thing occurred, I thought only of escape." That extempore friseur was never caught afterward with a pair of "thinning-scissors" in his hand !

A distinguished traveller mentions that in some instances in China, the "outside barbarians," are sometimes looked upon as gods, and at others as devils ; and lie mentions an absurd and very amusing story which goes to show the fear with which strangers are looked upon by this superstitious race: " After my friend had visited the Porcelain Tower, being somewhat fatigued, he stepped into a barber's shop, and by way of employing his time, he desired the barber to shave his head. The gentleman wore a wig, hut which, for the sake of coolness, he had placed in his pocket. This operation of shaving, so common in China, was speedily and skillfully executed, the barber seeming to be delighted with the honor of shaving one of the illustrious strangers. Previously to his leaving the shop, and while the man's attention was called in some other direction, my friend replaced his wig upon his head, little thinking of the result of his simple process. No sooner, however, had the barber turned round, and observed him whom lie had so lately cleaned of every vestige of hair, suddenly covered with a most luxuriant growth, than taking one steady gaze at him, to make sure that he was not deceived, he let fall the razor, cleared his counter at a hound, and running madly through the crowd which was speedily collected, cried by the devil ' out that he was visited " No entreaties could induce him to return, until every 'outside barbarian' had left the neighborhood ; so palpable a miracle as this being, in his opinion,
quite beyond the powers of all the gods and demons in the Buddhist calendar!"

New Remedy for Toothache. þÿ Mr. Jas. Beatson, of Airdrie, says þÿ Gum Copal, when dissolved in chloroform, forms an excellent compound for stuffing the holes of decayed teeth. I have used it very frequently, and the benefit which my patients have derived from it has been truly astonishing. The application is simple and easy. 1 clean out the hole, and moisten a little cotton with the solution; I introduce this into the decayed part, and in every instance the relief has been almost instantaneous. The chloroform removes the pain, and the gum copal resists the action of the saliva; and as the application is agreeable, those who may labour under this dreadful malady would do well to make a trial of it. þÿ Medical Times in Jour. The Morning Herald of Monday has the following statement on this subject, which, as that paper is regarded as the organ of the Government, is presumed to emanate " from authority :" þÿ In reference to a question which naturally at this moment absorbs the public attention both in England and in the United States the facts are as follows: þÿ Her Majesty's Government have made no new claims on the United States, and have withdrawn no concessions made to that Government. No renewal of the long-vexed question respecting the Bay of Fundy has been mooted. Lord Aberdeen's concession of 1845, respecting that arm of the sea (guarded as it was by bis Lordship by an assertion of our rights over the whole bay), remains where it was. The disputed interpretation of the technical terms of the treaty of 1818 remains where it was. All that has been done by the Government is to strengthen our squadron on the coast of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, to defend a right which the United States do not, and never did, dispute þÿ namely, that ot retaining excluin our possession the water within three miles of our own shores from the encroachments of both French and American fishermen ; and the American vessel, the Coral, alluded to, was seized within a quarter of a mile of our own coast. Our squadron is now no larger than the French one on the same coasts. Our right is that which demands the respect of all nations of the globe þÿ one acknowledged by international law; and

vernments have neglected te protect their fellow-subjects as France and the United States always protect theirs, both in America and in the Channel, we can only be grateful to our present Ministers for repairing their fatal supineness. We shall return to this subject, upon which, both here and across the Atlantic, the public have been most grossly misinformed and misled.

THE WEATHER! We notice (thanks to Divine Providence) the favorable change that has now taken place in the weather, which had been excessively warm for the last few weeks. The severe thunder and lightning, which we experienced here last Saturday night, have not done any injury, as far as we can learn the clouds þÿ that hung heavily then have been dispersed, and copious showers of rain have been the result. We sincerely hope that the Island will be favored by a continuance of good wcatber, so as to enable the planters to establish a good crop for next year ; as the cane fields were suffering much from the late dry weather.

From the Xew York Herald. The News. The difficulty with regard to the Eastern fisheries has become the chief topic ol discussion throughout the country. There appears to be but one voice as to the final result of the controversy, and that is, that the American fishermen must be protected in their just rights, let the consequences be what they may. Indeed, the afi'.iir seems to assume a more serious aspect every day ; and, unless a great deal of caution is exerconveniently arranged, on the part of our provincial neighbors, may really ter- cised by both governments, the finale of the flare-up minate more seriously than was at first apprehended. If the statement of the passengers and crew of the American schooner Lion, of Brookhaven, which was seized oil' Prince Edward Island, is correct, the British are certainly carrying things rather beyond their proper limits. Those on board of the Lion at the time, state that she was becalmed, and fidly three miles from the land. This must be inquired into with promptness, and if the story is correct, she must be released. from Boston, another schooner, the Florida, was captured and taken into Charlottetown, on the 5th instant. By the way, this subject will be the order of the day in the United States Senate next Thursday, when it is to be hoped that the whole matter will undergo a full, careful, and impartial examination. Mr. Soule, of Louisiana, it is whispered, is preparing a speech in which he will review the recent proceedings of Mr. Webster in a manner that will not

be very flattering to the gigantic capacity of the distinguished Secretary, who returned to his post yesterday. Our special Washington correspondent gives an outline ol a new kind of screw vessel of war, which tin- Naval Committee of the House have recently had under consideration, and are about to recommend for adoption. If the plan succeeds, it is probable that all our naval vessels will be provided with steam screw propellers. This would make our maritime defence very efficient.

The New York Crystal Palace. þÿ Under the active exertions of the association for carrying out this project, such progress has been made as promises to it a much higher degree of success and utility than has been hitherto anticipated for it. Circulars have been directed to the representatives of foreign countries, in New York, London and elsewhere, requesting the co-operation of their respective governments nations in this undertaking, and replies have been received by the President of the Association, conveying assurance of the great interest taken in this industrial scheme, and promising their sympathy and support. We publish, elsewhere in our columns, to-day, copies of some of those replies, received from the British, Portuguese, French, Austrian, and Bremen Consuls at New York, and from the Turkish Ambassador at London, which convey very strong expressions of the favorable manner in which the projected exhibition is regarded by their respective governments. That from the Ambassador of the Sublime Porte assures the Association that the matter has met with the high approbation of the Sultan, and that a government steamer will be specially deputed to convey to New York the contributions of the Ottoman Empire. We may therefore, indulge in the belief that the New York Crystal Palace Fair will be creditable, to this city and republic. A great number of plans and specifications for the edifice to be erected for the purpose in Reservoir square, have been sent in to the
