St. Thomas Times, September 4, 1852. OBITUARY. It is our painful duty to record this afternoon the death, from fever, in tne 27th year of his age, of the Reverend Edmund Richards, Minister of the Episcopal Church in this Island, which melancholy event took place at his late residence on the morning of the 3rd instant. The Revd. gentleman was born in Virginia, U. S., and arrived in this Colony in the month of November last year, when he assumed the responsible functions of his ecclesiastical office, and much credit is due to the memory of the deceased for the affectionate and tender care of his flock, his watchful eye over his congregation and his zeal and patience in bringing sinners to God. As a Pastor, he was beloved, and as a Christian, respected and esteemed The intelligence of his early demise in a foreign clime will be sad news to a dear and tender mother, and a kind and fond sister, whom he has left behind in his native land. His remains were taken to the Church last evening, and there laid out for the mournful satisfaction of those who wished to view his last, until this morning, when they were removed to their last resting place, accominhabitants. þÿ panied by an " immense concourse of all classes of the Blessed be the dead that die in the IiOrd."

OFFICE OF THE Association tor the Exhibition of the Industry of all Nations. New-York, 12th July, 1852. THE ASSOCIATION FOR THE EXHIBI- TION OF THE INDUSTRY OF ALL NATIONS give notice that the Exhibition will be opened, in the City of New-York, on the 2d day of May, 1853. The Municipal Anthorities have granted to them the use of Reservoir Square, and they are proceeding to erect thereon a Building worthy of the purpose to which it is to be devoted. The Association desire to make the Exhibition, in fact as well as in name, a Representation from other countries as well as their own, of Raw Materials and Produce, Manufactures, Machinery and Fine Arts. To this end they have made arrangements with Charles Buschek, Esquire, late Commissioner of the Austrian Empire at the Industrial Exhibition of London, whose skill, experience and high character offer the most satisfactory security to Contributors from abroad. Mr. Buschek is the authorized Agent of this Association, for all countries other than the Continent of America, and as such has received its instructions. All communications from Contributors abroad must bs addressed to him at "The Office of the Exhibition of the Industry of all Nations in New-York," No. 6 Charing Cross, London. He will state to them the nature of the powers given and authority conferred, and will also explain the great inducements offered by this Enterprise to European Exhibitors. This Association will correspond with all persons in the United States, the Canadas and British Provinces,

the West Indies and this Continent generally, who mav desire to contribute to this Exhibition. All such communications must be addressed to " The Secretary of the Association for the Exhibition of the Industry of all Nations, New- York." The Association is now ready to receive applications, and it is desired that they be sent in immediately. Due notice will be given, hereafter, when the Building will be ready for the reception of articles. Applications for the admission of Objects to the Exhibition must represent intelligibly their nature and purpose, and must also state distinctly the number of Square Feet, whether of Wall, Floor or Counter, required. Machinery will be exhibited in þÿMotion the Motive Power to be furnished by the Association þÿ and applications for the Admission of Machinery, to be so exhibited, in addition to the general description and the requisition for space, must set forth the amount of Motive Power required. The Association deem it proper to announce that Paintings in Frames will be exhibited. As, notwithstanding the magnitude of the proposed Building, there must, necessarily, be a limitation of space, the Association reserves the right to modify or reject applications, but, in so doing, will be governed by strict impartiality, looking only to the general objects of the Enterprise. The Association also reserves the right of determining the length of time, not to exceed in any case one season, during which objects shall, severally, form part
cf the Exhibition.

8 T Ut 0 VL ATI3, Exhibitors are requested to designate an Agent to whom their contributions shall be delivered when withdrawn from the Exhibition. Prizes for Excellence in the various departments of the Exhibition will be awarded under the direction of Capable and Eminent Persons. With this statement the Directors solicit the co-operation of the Productive Intellect and Industry of their own and other Countries. THEODORE SEDGWICK, President. Win. Whetten, Secretary. DIRECTORS. The "Port of Spain Gazette," of the 16th August, contains the particulars of a melancholy accident, attended with loss of life, which occurred on board the Steamer Victoria, on the 14th : " The steamer proceeded on Wednesday last on her customary daily trip to and Iro n San Fernando, and arrived off that town, at her usual hour, without anything occurring indicative of the calamity which was so speedily to follow; and having discharged tier passengers, and taken in those wl.o proposed proceeding by her to Port of Spain, again got under weigh (at 3 p. in.), and had reached about half way between Pointe-a-Pierre and the Lodge Estate, when a noise as of an explosjon was heard by those on board, and great quantities of steam rushed up from below, through the hatchway. The crew and fore-deck passengers, many of them severely scalded by the steam which had forced its way upon deck, made for the after part of the vessel, where the boats of the steamer were hanging by the davits, and in so doing had to cross through the escaping steam, and suffered yet more severely. The after or cabin passengers had, in the mean time, rushed to the stern of the vessel, and fortunately escaped the action of the steam. » " In the mean time the steamer had been brought to an anchor, and the vapour from below had sufficiently dispersed to allow the melancholy sight of the two stokers lying dead, and although Africans, their corpses presented the appearance, from the scalding off of the

eperdeinis, of two white men, the hair and who features had only denoting the negro. Two boys also (black) been down in the hold at the time, presented a lamentable spectacle, their skins having peeled off wherever the flesh was exposed þÿ but they were as yet alive. " The deaths and casualties, as far as is yet known, arc as follows Two men drowned. Two Stokers killed on the spot. Two boys, who have died in San Fernando Hospital. Cyrus (Steward) since dead. Two women are very dangerously scald d, not expected to recover ; two or tnree otliers are seriously injured."

Wilmcr and Smith's European Times, August 16, 1852. Australian Rigging. Advices have arrived by the Stebonhcath, from Port Philip direct, to the 22nd April. It appears that the production at the mines was steadily increasing, and was no w estimated at £, 100, 000 per week, or at the rate of more than £5,000,000 per annum for this colony alone. The present vessel has hronght about 60,000 ounces, valued at £230,000; and the Vanguard, which sailed a few days previously, hut which has not yet arrived, took 17,490 ounces, nearly £70,000 worth. The quotation was 60s. to 61s. per ounce. Great complaints continue to he made of the prevalence of crime, owing to the influx of convicts from Van Diemen's Land, many of whom were among I he most successful people tit the mines. Bain had begun to fall at Mount Alexander, but not so as to increase ihe facilities for working, and in the other districts it was still delayed. The statement of the public revenue of the colony for the quarter had created both satisfaction and surprise, the increase being £95,592 ; a sum nearly equal to the whole public revenue of the corresponding front of this arose quarter the duties on spirits, of last year. Much tobacco, and foreign goods. In the territorial revenue, likewise, there was an extraordinary augmentation. For the corresponding quarter of 1851 the total of that revenue was £9,138, and now it was £156,827; the chief items of increase being the land sales, which

amounted to £95,248 ; the gold licenses, which produced £48,597 ; and the gold escort, which produced £4489. The rate for bills on England was about 8£ to 10 per cent, discount. A letter from Melbourne says : "The þÿ total population at the diggings is estimated by the chief commissioner at about 35,000, but a considerable portion is migratory, and not half that number of licensesare issued. The present weekly produce cannot be under 30,000 ounces, or about £100,000 in value, as the Government escort alone now brings down about 20,000 oz., independent of the large quantity conveyed privately. From a | after the post-office to the river Loddon, distance of six or seven miles, the bed and slopes of Forest Creek present the appearance of being covered with a series of gigantic molehills, interspersed with miserable small tents of every description, the occupants of which have a very squalid, unhealthy appearance, from exposure, privation, and dust, sore eyes being universally prevalent. The roads are now very bad, the cost ot carriage from Melbourne being £22 to £25 a ton ; but most people are of opinion that, when the rain falls, in about a month, they will be all but impassable, and serious apprehensions are entertained of a scarcity of food during the winter months. The gold is found both in deposit and in the matrix, a quartz vein having been struck at about twenty or thirty feet below the surface, and traced for some distance, which is worked successfully with no other tools or ma-

chinery than pickaxe, hammer, and tin dish. It has also been found in deposit in various strata of alluvial earth, clay, and gravel, and even below the trap rock, leaving little room to doubt that the supply is not likely to be soon exhausted ; while the Mitta-Mitta Fields, near the boundary of the colon v, on the M urray, are still all but untried.

The Secret Treaty. þÿ We are enabled to state that the Convention alleged to have been concluded by the Three Great Northern Powers of Europe, and which was published in its ipissima verba by a contemporary., the Morning Chronicle, in the course of the week, has not been completed in the form in which it has been printed, nor indeed in any substantial form whatever as a formal public act. þÿ Observer. þÿ The Cologne Gazette, in a telegraphic despatch from Berlin, states that the Prussian Gazette declares the secret convention of the Northern Powers published in the Morning Chronicle to be a mere fabrication.

Horrible Murder in Spain. þÿ A great deal of excitement prevails at present in the province of Andalusia, in Spain, in consequence of the discovery of a great crime. A goat-keeper, named Tradilla, lived with his wife and ten children in a lonely part of the mountains of Alcala. He conceived a violent passion for one of his daughters, named Maria Josefa, aged 13. She rejected his advances with horror, and frequent quarrels took place between them. At length, to get out of the reach of her father, the poor girl determined to marry. She accordingly, some time ago, got young a farm

®S©12 AT I 3. i labourer, named Antonio de los Kios, to whom she had some time been attached, to demand her hand of her father. This he did, and Tradilla received him with great apparent courtesy, made him stop all day, and at night provided him a sleeping-place in a barn. were When the together what visitor and all the family plunged in sleep, Tradilla rose, slipped to the barn, and bound the legs and arms of Antonio. He then cut his throat with a large razor. He afterwards knocked up his eldest son, named Pedro, and told him to go to deep a ravine at some distance, and dig a hole. Pedro shortly arrived with his spade and pickaxe | at the place indicated, and there found his father with the dead body of Antonio. The young man started with horror, but Tradilla rudely told him to dig a grave for the victim. He at first refused, but intimidated by the dreadful threats of his father, he set to work. As, however, he did not get on fast enough, Tradilla knocked up his wife and all his children, and madt; them help him. Maria was amongst them. On seeing the body of her lover she tainted, but her father beat her until she recovered, and then took a sort of malignant pleasure in compelling her to work at the grave. From this time Maria could not bear the sight of her father, and he frequently shamefully ill-treated her. þÿ One day, a fortnight back, he tied her to a tree and beat her most severely. Her cries attracted her mother, brothers, and some peasants to the spot. On seeing them Tradilla took to flight, lie

was pursued, but when the pursuers were about to seize him he resisted furiously, and struck right and lett Willi a large ® stick. In ... so doing he broke the arm of one of his little children. Eventually he escaped, and secreted himself troved in the process. Athenaeum. among the rocks. His son Pedro informed the local authorities of the crimes committed by his father. They sent a strong detachment of the civic guard to search the mountains, and after a while Tradilla was secured and safely lodged in the gaol of Medina-Sidonia. He readily confessed his guilt, and is to be brought to trial in the course of the month. The body of his victim was dug up, and after being recognised was interred in the cemetry.

The Cure, hearing of the circumstance, immediately repaired to the spot. But what could lie do, being alone, without remedies, and far from any medical man. The poison would have been fully absorbed ; and time pressed. A thought occurred to him, it was at once to open and suck the wound. Disregarding the danger of such a proceeding, and notwithstanding the repugnance which such a means must have caused, the Cure made no hesitation. He sucked the wound and drew from it a glass and a half of blood, and along with that blood the poison which would have been the cause of most dreadful agonies, and probably of death. In the meantime a Doctor arrived, who lauded the firm resolution of the Cure, admired his courage in so hazardous a proceeding, and went away saying there was nothing more to be done, the best of remedies having been already employed. The result was, that on the following day, with the exception of a slight swelling of the part, the young man was quite well." In a process of this kind, the operator must, for his own safety possess a sound mouth, free from bad gums, or sore or tender flesh in those parts.. PROVERBS. There are a good many prove-bs that will not stand a very close analysis ; and some one who is of this way of thinking has selected a few examples, by way of illustration. The following are specimens : " The more the merrier." þÿ Not so, " by a jug-full," one hand, for example, is quite enough in a purse. " He that runs fastest gets most ground. ' þÿ Not exactly ; for then footmen would get more than their masters. " He runs far who never turns." þÿ Not quite : he may break his neck in a short course. " No man can call again yesterday." þÿ Yes, he may call till his heart a he, though it may never co.ne. A correspondent w rites þÿ " He that goes softly goes safely." þÿ Not, among thieves. " Nothing hurts the stomach more than surfeiting." þÿ Yes ; lack of meat. " Nothing is hard to a willing þÿmind." Surely ; for every body is willing to get money, but to many it is hard. "None so blind as those that will not see." þÿ Yes; those who can not see. þÿ " Nothing but wlift is good for something." þÿ "Nothing" isn't good for any thing. " Nothing hut what has an end." þÿ A ring hath no end ; for it is round. " Money is a great comfort." þÿ But not when it brings a thief to the State Prison. " The world is a long journey." þÿ Not always ; for the sun goes over it every day. " It is a great way to the bottom of the sea." þÿ Not at all ; it is merely " a stone's throw." "A friend is best found in adversity." þÿ "No sir;" for then there are none to be found. " The pride of the rich makes the labor of the poor."
þÿ By no manner of means. The labor of the poor makes the pride of the rich.

57. Thomas Times . 22, 1852. The Gale ! The Sun entering Libra at twenty-five minutes after 6 o'clock on the afternoon of the 22nd, and the Moon having entered her first-quarter ou the 20th, gave reasonable cause for anxiety to the Inhabitants that bad weather could be apprehended, and which, in this instance, was rather unhappily confirmed. The Barometer commenced to fall on the afternoon of Wednesday, and indicated the approach of a storm or hurricane, which however did not commence before about 4 o'clock on the morning of the 23rd, and gradually increased until 9 o'clock, when most of the Barometers þÿ as compared afterwards þÿ had fallen five lines. The gale came from the W. N. W ; and by Colonel Reid's Theory of Storms, St. Thomas must have stood on the outside of the circle. A gale from that direction exposes our harbour more than the town, which latter is considerably sheltered by the high hills immediately at its back. In the town, we have not many casualties to chronicle, as the injuries sustained consist of some galleries attached to the front of dwellings having blown away, roofs partially stripped of their tiles and slates, fences and trees blown down, and two of the pillars which supported the wooden rails around the Reform Dutch Church were also thrown down. In the harbour, the accidents are of a far more serious character; tlte shipping, which by good fortune were few, have sustained much injury: the Spanish brigantine Delores la Perla foundered immediately in front ol the

Marine Slip; the Spanish sloop Sin Antonio also foundered opposite the ship-yard of Captain Daniel þÿ fore, probable, that a more extensive and remunerative both of these will require considerable outlay to be raised; the French brig Matliilde, of Havre, which had just arrived from Martinique, in ballast, parted from her anchors at about 10 o'clock in the morning, and ran ashore at the point under Havensigt Hill, and opposite l'rince Rupert's Rocks, where she soon after became a total wreck. Fortunately the whole of her crew were saved through the able management of her com., captain Wannebkoncq, in getting the boats out, and preventing them being dashed to pieces on the rocks. In the morning, the Mathilde proudly rode the waters, full of buoyancy, in the afternoon she was a complete þÿwreck, affording us a forcible and truthful illustration of human life. The American brigs Julia Ridgway and Thomas Trowbridge have both received great damage from the French barque Revanche, which parted her cables, and ran into each of tlieui with such force as to cause the three to drift to the East end of the harbour. An unfortunate young porter met with a watery grave the same day, by recklessly jumping overboard to pick up a panama hat that had been blown from off the head of a gentleman, and fell into the Water. Tlie poor fellow reached his object, but alas, nature became exhausted, and he was drowned before reaching the shore. His body was found yesterday afternoon. We have not heard of any fur-
ther loss of life.

St. Thomas Times, Sept. 25, 1852. Santo Domingo. The following Regulations for the Port of Santo Domingo, which may be

!r & t i of interest to our readers, we copy from Art. J. All masters of vessels arriving from foreign parts, shall deliver to the Pilot who boards them all the letters and newspapers destined for this port, with the exception of the consignees' letters. It shall be optional to the master to take the pilot or not, to anchor the vessels in the roads, or bring her into iort. Art. 2. .The Master shall produce to the Health Officer, on receiving bis visit, the corresponding Bill of Health, and cause all Ins crew and passengers to appear and be seen by the Officer. Art. 3. After the vessel is brought to an anchor, a visit shall be paid by the Olficers of the Customs and Harbour, to whom the master shall deliver the vessel's Register, and a Manifest of the entire cargo, clearing up the places where the seals are to be fixed, and permitting the Officer on duty to remain on board until the vessel is discharged. Art. 4. All vessels having cargo or ballast to discharge, shall be placed at the spot where they are to unload, by the Pilot that brings them to an anchor, and shall in no case change place unless previously authorized by the Harbour Master. Art. 5. All masters of vessels in the roads, or in port , are prohibited from throwing overboard any ballast or filth, and shall in case of necessity apply to the Harbour Master, in order that he may appoint the place discharge. to Art. 6. In order to obtain a coast-pilot, and the requisite journeymen, the masters of vessels that are to load on tne coast, accompanied by their consignees,

shall apply to the Harbour Master, who shall procure the men required, and in whose presence they shall be bound, and their advances paid. Art 7. On the visit previous to sailing, the masters of vessels are bound to present to the Harbour Master, the passports of the passengers that may be on board, and, before setting sail to deliver up the fort-pass to the man-of-war on station. SIMON CORSO, Harbour Master.

A Man without Money. þÿ A man without money is a body without life, a walking shadow, a spectre that affrights. His look is doleful, his conversation is languid and heavy. If he wishes to pay a visit, he never finds any body at home, and if he opens his mouth to speak, he is interrupted every moment, in order that he may not finish a sentence, lest he should end it by asking for money. He is avoided as a pestilence, anckis considered a useless clog upon the face of the earth. If he have wit, he cannot display it ; and if he have none, he is looked upon as the most frightful biped that nature can create. When in ill-humour, his enemies say he is fit for nothing ; and those best inclined towards him, preface their eulogy by a shrug of the shoulders. Necessity awakes hint in the morning, and misery attends bint to bed at night. The women find that he is unmannerly and vulgar, and regard him with suspicion. Tavernkeepers wish that, like the chameleon, be would live on air, and tailors that, like our first parents, lie would clothe himself with fig-leaves. If he wishes to argue, he is not listened to ; ami if he sneezes, he is not heard ; if he wants any thing from a tradesman, he is asked to pay beforehand ; and, if in debt, he is considered a rogue. A Temperance Preacher. þÿ Wine being common and cheap, the Germans so do not encourage distillation to the same extent as in other countries. What pro-

gress temperance societies may have the Gazeta de Gubierno, of that place: þÿ made remains to be ascertained, but, if the following anecdote be authentic, it affords a curious specimen of the opinions entertained by some German divines on the subject of intemperance. In a sermon preached by one, he exclaimed, that " intemperance consisted in passing these bounds which nature had prescribed. It was intemperance for men who were quarrelsome in their cups ever to drink wine. To some a goblet was refreshment, to others it caused sickness, and such were intemperate, when they drank more than one. Many enlivened society, and were kind when they had drunk four bottles, and it was not right in them to drink less. Many more felt their hearts warm with gratitude to the Deity as the generous juice circulated in their veins, when they had drunk eight bottles: þÿ with them intemperance began at the ninth." These persons he pronounced to be the peculiar favourites of heaven ; and, bowing todiis congregation, he acknowledged with fervour that he himself was one of these highly-gifted mortals.

St. Thomas Times, September 8, 1852. THE WEATHER, For some time past, has been hot and sultry; and on Sunday morning last, between 6 and 7 þÿo clock, the wind rose in fearful gusts, with heavy showers, for about half an hour. At one time, from the threatening appearance of the sky to the North-eastward, and the quick motion of the low clouds, we were apprehensive that a gale was coming on, but about nine þÿo clock the Barometer rose considerably, till about noon, when the weather again assumed a threatening aspect for a short time, but soon cleared up. With the strengtli of the wind, the sea rose somewhat, and caused trifling injury to a few of the wharves. Several fences were thrown down, and a number of trees destroyed, in town ; tile American barque Souliot, ice vessel, dragged her cables, and þÿ stuck in the þÿmud. The Signal Telegraph at Cowþÿell Battery s was also much damaged, the upper part being entirely blown off; hut the most melancholy circumstance which we have to report connected with the weather, is the loss of life of one man, who was drowned in his endeavour to preserve a Lighter belonging to a mercantile firm in this place. The deceased, who was an active boatman, fell overboard, and never rose again. His body was found on the following day. We look for some unpleasant ne>s from abroad.

Barbados vs. Jamaica. From the Jamaica Morning Journal, August 26.

the 20ih ult- the Attorney General of the In the Barbados House of Assemblv, on . island having moved the second reading of the þÿSavings Bank Bill, which was agreed to. and the h mse having gone into Committee on t tie said bill, his honor the Speaker, who opposed the measure, used rhe following observations, in reference to the distressed slate of the island of Jamaica. 1 i is Honor said. " We had before us the example of the once prosperous colony of Jamaica, which was now reduced to such a lamentable condition thai this year the whole amount of its produce, lie find been credibly informed, would be insufficient to meet its taxation. If this house went on raising up new institutions, entailing upon us additional expense without the justifications of unavoidable necessity, the time might come when our accumulated burthens might be so great that we should find ourselves reduced to a position similar to that of Jamaica. In the present condition of these colonies, he maintained that they were not justified in imposing any permanent burthens upon themselves which were not unavoidable. It was no answer to this, in his opinion, well founded objection, to say that the colony was just now in a very prosperous condition ; it was impossible to say how long their prosperity would last, or how soon it would pass away. Jamaica was once as prosperous as she was now depressed ; and it was impossible to say what would be the fate of our own colony in the course of a few years. If this bill had origina-

ted in an unavoidable necessity he should support it, but as it did not, he felt it his duty to oppose þÿit. To this the Attorney General replied as follows: þÿ þÿ His honorable þÿfriend (theSpeak- s er's) reference to Jamaica was rather unfortunate. because it was comparing a colony which had been, in a most signal manner, the receipt of the blessings of mercy with one that was sadly and sorely afflicted. It was saying, because Jamaica was distressed Barbados should not therefore be thankful and grateful for the advantages, benefits, and blessings received, and that we should not furihei merit a continuance of those blessings by endeavouring to make our laboring population a contented, a thriving and an industrious þÿpeasantry. Such an argument he could not concur in. such logic he was unable to understand. Having already stated to the house the reasons why he looked upon this measure as one of great importance, he confessed he was utterly surprised to find any member who looked at the extent and growth of the pauperism throughout the country hesitating for one moment to join in doing all that was in the power of legislation to do, to check this growing evil, by teaching the laboring classes to provide for the exigencies of sickness and old age. One great object of the measure was to prevent the parishes being overwhelmed by the number of poor. They could not maintain themselves, their families could not maintain them, because, heretofore, and even at this moment,

tlies were not a thoughtful, a thrifty, a steadv nor an iii'lusirmns population. And if the house sviis a-ked to contribute something from an ove flowing treasury towards perfecting a measure in which the interests of the island were involved, they were not asked to do too much He was the last man in that house to propose anything calculated to bring down the revenue to an amount less than the expenditure; he would be one of the first to suffer by such an act. But, at the present moment, when we knew that we had a considerable surplus in hand, when we knew that our annual revenue considerably exceeded our expenditure, lie wanted to know what comparison there was between

this Island and Jamaica. He (Mr. Sealy) had understood that the actual value of this whole crop this year would not be sufficient to pay its taxes. Was that a colony to compare with this ? Were we to do nothing for our laboring population to whom we were so much indebted for our comparatively thriving condition ; or, on the other hand, were we to suffer them to lapse into a comparative state of batbarism by begrudging £200 or £300 a year, for adding in the sustentation of a measure of this description? He (Mr S.) regretted exceedingly that this measure should have been opposed ; still such grounds þÿ more, that it should have been opposed on The Bill ultimately passed the committee, and the House having resumed, it was read a third time and passed. »«« London Times, August 1(5, 1852.

Fisheries and Seamen. TO THE EDITOR OF THE TIMES. Sir, þÿ Were not the question of maintaining our nurseries for seamen more important than commercial considerations þÿ(Smith Wealth s of Nations, vol. iv., c. 2) I should not again venture, through your favour, to trespass on public attention regarding the North American fisheries; hut, perceiving that impressions are likely to be made by writers, avoiding responsibility for erroneous opinions by withholding their names, I feel it a duty explicitly to state that þÿ it is not to the amount offish caught and cured, to the price tit which it can he sold at home or abroad, or to the number of persons employed in the fishery, but to their nationality and vocation to which I attach importance, in order that our fisheries shall lorni hardy British seamen in oceanic vessels, like those employed under the bounties paid by North America and France. These being the considerations, the question is not whether it is consistent with the enlightened theory of free trade to pay a premium which shall transfer capital from the pockets of one class to those of another, but whether it is wiser and more economical for the community at large to uphold such nursery, or to maintain, even a skeleton of warlike establishments þÿ perhaps to build, equip, and employ additional ships-of-war, squadrons, or fleets to watch, perchance to contend with, power thus cheaply developed by rival nations. Again, 1 ask, notwithstanding anonymous criticism, whether the bounty

given to enable steampackets to cross the ocean is more consistent with free trade principles than a bounty awarded to our fisheries as a nursery for seamen ? A colonial premium is indeed talked of, and by those unacquainted witli facts, who do not foresee its operation, it may he deemed a substitute for a bounty by the parent State ; but I advisedly assert that such colonial premium would not rear one disposable seaman for our naval service, and that even the colonial fishermen would derive no commensurate advantage, such is the impoverishing effect of the inveterate system of truck-dealing, that boat fishermen, even from the harbour of the capital of Newfoundland are chiefly paid by daily wages; the advantages, derived front the employment of two half idle fishermen, being greater to the truckmaster (in the absence of an available market) than the like amount of fish caught by one customer! It is manifest, by the true theory of free trade, that it is unimportant whether the French and Americans obtain their bait, and catch fish within our limits or not, or even whether the world is supplied by them or by us ; but it is not so, if foreign nations thereby rear, employ, and maintain in time of peace 50,000 sea-

men, who, in the event of war, are at the beck of their respective Governments, while Britain (rightful owner) has not one available seaman from the fisheries ! On subjects of such vital importance it is essential that general theories, however good, shall not be supported in detail by false reasoning, or by captivating appellations inconsistent with truth. Nine-tenths of our western colonies are still taxed on every article of food, and on all existing property, animate, and inanimate; a state of things alike adverse to production and trade. Is it reasonable to imagine, if the interests of colonists are not considered jointly with those of the parent State, that they can continue to administer to our wants, comforts, and luxuries þÿ above all to our commercial nursery for seamen, the source of our national greatness? A Parliamentary investigation is indispensable to afford a chance of escape to these noble possessions of the Crown from impending ruin. I am, Sir, grateful for your favours in a public as well as private point of view, Your obedient servant, Dundonald.

The I-'reneli at Tripoli. The following is taken from a letter, dated þÿ Tripoli, the 1st þÿinstant. þÿ : þÿ Our proceedings have been very warlike of late. I mentioned in my last the fact of two deserters from the Algerine French army having entered the service of the Pasha, from which they had deserted and had been arrested, but claimed by the French consul. I did not, however, mention that, having been disowned by the French consul ns his subjects, they had renounced allegiance to France and declared allegiance to the Ottoman Empire before the þÿ þÿMiglis, or Provincial Council, according to established usage, were mustered into the service, and served five months. One was employed by special order from Constantinople, at $12 a-month, as a veterenary surgeon; the the other at $8, to shoe the cavalry horses. þÿ Having been strongly taken to task by the Romish priests for abandoning their religion, they finally wore persuaded to desert from the Turkish service, as before related. After their capture they w'ere treated as deserters, but still with every kind of leniency. In three þÿweeks time they were liberated, and then did they deeply regret having claimed the protection of the French. They said they were persuadfd bv the priests, who assured them they would be sent to Rome, and be allowed to enter the French army there, with a full pardon for their desertion from Algiers, if they would claim the protection of the consul. They now, however, feared they should be sent to France, and there shot or be sent to tbe hulks. Reports were rife

as to the humanity of the Turks to the men, and a report was made to that effect to the Cormnander-in- Chief, who, to judge for himself, ordered the men before him. They came, acknowledged they had been misled by the priests, that they were desirous of continuing in the Turkish service, that they had been treated far more leniently than they deserved, and, in fine, that they deeply regretted their desertion. þÿ Things were in this state when the Corner French steam frigate arrived at Tripoli on the 22d of July. þÿ On her arrival the consul demanded the delivery of the men before sunset. The Pasha, who had gone to Bengazi, was represented by the Mudir, who replied that, as the whole question had been referred to Constantinople for the þÿSultan decision, s he could not surrender the men, and he, the Mudir, hoped the consul would allow the French Legation at the Porte to entertain the question. The þÿMitdir l s etter was in every pomt respectful. þÿ On receipt of the Mudir's reply, the consul commenced his preparations for embarking with his family of proteges, priests, and residents, with all the valuables of the church (silver &c.), on board the Conner. People became alarmed, and several left the regency. þÿ On the 28th, a French squadron of six sail of the line, a steam frigate, and two steam corvettes, hove in sight, and were seen bearing down for the city. þÿ To describe tbe scene that followed is impossible, mon, women, and children Hying to the Marina for safety on board the vessels in the roads, of which all

were put into requisition, and were soon crowded with fugitives. þÿ The fleet bore down, and soon took up their distance around the walls of the town, forming a cordon of the most imposing nature. þÿ In the afternoon the consul sent his þÿultimatum viz., that if the men were not given up by sunrise of the 29th on board the flagship of Admiral de la Susac, recourse would be had to force. þÿ At half-past 6 p. m., on the 28th, a circular was addressed by the French consul to his colleagues, announcing the intention of resorting to force in the 1

a 'Jt x> 'i z: Avn 3 morning, and oftering an asylum to them and the people claiming their protection on board the squadron. þÿ The English, American, and Dutch consul, not approving the proceedings of the French consul, and thinking the time allowed far too short to take measures for tbe security of the lives and property of their subjects, determined on a correspondence with the admiral and consul on the subject. While so occupied, they were visited by the Spanish, Austrian, Neapolitan, and Tuscan consuls, who, fearfully intimidated, prayed, the three first named, to join them in a visit to the authorities to endeavour to persuade them to give up the men and save the town. After some time the American consul addressed them thus : þÿ þÿ þÿ I agree with you that the French squadron can reduce the town to powder in half an hour. But if I it, to the lowest depths of ... I would not advise knew that they would send the town and every soul in . the governor to give up the þÿmen. No more was said by the four dignitaries. þÿ At sunrise on the 29th the men were not given up ; the consul hauled down his colours, and, with his family and his subjects, went on board tbe ships. Just at this time a message was sent by the acting governor to the foreign consuls, begging them to attend a conference at the Palace on the state of a Hairs, and they met accordingly. þÿ The Mudir opened the conference, by a concise statement, as follows : þÿ þÿ The Pasha, before going to Bengazi, had positively refused the extradition of the two men ; that they had

renounced their allegiance to France, and had adhered to that of the Ottoman Empire, long before they were claimed by the consul; that they were now unwilling to be given up to the consul; that they were at large in the streets, and could had gone to him or to the squadron whenever they wished to do so; and, in consideration of these facts, the Government was very strougly opposed to the surrender of the men. þÿ On the other hand, the Mudir stated that the time allowed for their delivery on board had expired, and that an immediate attack from the ships was expected. The town was wholly indefensible against such a lorce, and in case of attack its destruction was inevitable. The population had therefore implored the Government to sureender the men, as the only means of avoiding the calamitous consequences ; and he (the acting governor) therefore requested our advice on the subject. þÿ The various consuls gave different opinions, of which, however, I am not in possession. The United States' consul (and throughout the business the English and Dutch agreed with him) said as follows : þÿ of the group between Mars and þÿ þÿ It is quite impossible for me in any case to advise the forcible extradition of a man from a country which he has adopted as his own, and to which he had solemnly sworn allegiance. I agree entirely in the opinion that an attack will be made if the men are not given up, and that the town will probably be demolished. But a great principle is involved in this case,

and it is a question Worthy of the most serious consideration, whether the principle is not worth more than the town. For myself, or my own personal security, an asylum has been offered me on board the ships of the squadron; but I shall deem it my duty to remain at my post and take whatever may come. On the other hand, the suffering which would occur to the unoffending population, in case the town was bombarded, should have great weight with those Who decide the question ; and, while I cannot assume the responsibility of advising the surrender or non-surrender of the men, under all the circumstances, I would advise the authorities, if they should decide on giving them up, to do so under a solemn protest, in writing, setting forth the reasons which had led to the act, distinctly reserving the principle which they had maintained from the beginning, and adding, that as the town was quite indefensible against such a force as that with which it was threatened, the authorities had yielded to the claims of þÿhumanity. þÿ The above suggestions were adopted, the men were surrendered under protest, and the authorities declared they yielded to superior force, leaving open the question of right to bo decided by the Governments of Turkey and France. þÿ The Admiral, having refused to interfere in other matters of quarrel between the Consul and the Pasha, gave him the Gomer to convey him to Malta. The French flag is still down, and all other points at issue are in statu þÿquo. þÿ Ibid.

Fine Writers and fine Talkers. þÿ Fine writers are sometimes, not always, tine talkers ; a man may be incomparable as a talker, yet insignificant as a writer. The distinction we take to be this : þÿ In the fine writer we have intellect disengaged from the emotions, and dealing freely with its subject with such mastery as is given to it ; in the fine taiker the intellect moves in alliance with the emotions, and deals with its subject, not according to the demands of the subject, but according to the impulses of the feelings, so that, instead of mastering the subject, the talker is mastered by his emotions : he gives utterance to what he feels , if he feels strongly, he communicates that to us. We have little time to scan and scrutinize his reasons ; we are captivated by an image, startled by an epigram, puzzled by a paradox, borne down by eye, gesture, voice; we quit bun dazzled, delighted with a souse of his power ; we speak of his brilliant talk, and, if we try to remember any thing he said, it seems so poor and insignificant, that we should as soon think of quoting it as of presenting the rocket-stick to one who had never seen the climbing splendour of the rocket in the night air.

The clearances from the port of London for the gold colonies of Australia for the week ending August 7, consisted of seven ships to Port Philip, of an aggregate capacity of 3003 tons (besides an East Indiaman of 1292 tons, freighted in part for that colony), and of four ships to Sydney, of 2048 tons, exclusive of the mail steamer Sydney. There was also one vessel of 835 tons to Adelaide, South Australia. The exports of manufactured goods, as well as of wines, spirits, and tobacco, were again large, although emigrants at present constitute the chief portion of Australian cargoes, the number of these for the week having probably been from 1200 to 1500. Among the miscellaneous exports were two rather large consignments of hops.

A Somnambulist. þÿ A Bordeaux journal states that a wealthy farmer, in the neighbourhood of that city, lately perceived that some of his fowls and pigeons were stolen. As two enormous dogs were let loose in the farmhouse at night, it was supposed that the theft must have been committed by some persons in the house. The farmer, in consequence, determined to post his men in various places in the premises the next night, and have a strict watch kept. The men remained at their posts until a little after 12, when the noise of a key turning in a lock was heard, and the moment after the farmer himself made his appearance in his shirt and evidently in a state of somnambulism. He proceeded straight to the pigeon house, twisted the necks of two birds, and carried them off with him. He did the same to two ducks, and then returned tranquilly to his own room, where he hid the birds carefully in a press, and went to bed. This occurrence being related the next day to the sons, they adopted measures to prevent it taking place again.

After the 1853 every person, entering into any engagement as servant, either as domestic servant or for the performance of any other work, in which servants, engaged for a certain period, are employed, (for instance as journeyman in a warehouse, or for carrying about goods for sale) shall be provided with a serving-book (Tjeneste-bog) to be obtained in the police office of the jurisdiction. This book shall contain a printed extract from the present ordinance, and shall therein be entered, under the hand of the respective Police Magistrate, the full name, birthplace

and age of the recipient (the age according to the best of the Police þÿ.Magistrate s judgment, if it cannot be given with accuracy) and, moreover, the lormer position or livelihood of the concerned, if he or she has been in possession of any. The books shall be procured for account of the Land Treasury. $ 2. All servants, entering upon any service, shall within 48 hours give attendance in the police office of the jurisdiction and produce their serving-books, in which the Police Magistrate shall then, according to the servant's own statement, enter, where and by whom, in what capacity and for what term lie or she has been engaged. The above as well as all other terms agreed upon may, however, also be entered by the master, under his own hand, and in this case the Police shall only add a notice to the effect, that the above entry has been produced in the police office. Any servant, quitting his or her service, shall be bound to produce, within the same term, the book in the police office, in order that the change, which has taken place in the position of the same, may be noted therein. Ant- servant, leaving a police jurisdiction for the purpose of entering upon service in any other, shall, in compliance with the above, inform thereof the police offices of both jurisdictions. 3. Persons, engaged by the year on any Estate and employed as domestic servants by the proprietor or manager of the same Estate shall be exempted from being provided with serving-books. This rule applies also to

children under 13 years of age. $ 4 I he master may, whenever a servant quits his service, enter, at the request of the latter, in the book, his testimony of the ability and conduct of the same, during the time of service, and for the tenor of such testimony the master shall be answerable. 5. Servants are bound carefully to keep their serving-books ; but the master may demand, at any time, to see the books of his servants In case a book should be lost, the owner shall without delay report it to the respective Police Magistrate, who will then make the necessary inquiry on the subject. Should it be requisite t(f issue a new book, the Police Magistrate shall enter therein the cause, that has occasioned this, together with such information of the former condition of the individual in question, as can be obtained. M The Police shall keep a register of all serving-books, that have been issued and produced. The engagement or dismissal of any servant shall be reported by the master to the police, within 48 hours, and this rule is also applicable to the servants mentioned in 3 who are exempted from being provided with books. In case the servant does not reside with his or her employer, this must be specially mentioned when the report is made. Individuals whose daily work is not entirely at the disposal of the reported master, or who besides their services have other employment, shall not when the question arises how far the individual according to 2 of the law of this þÿday d s ate, regarding vagrancy in the

Danish West India Possessions, has lawful maintenance, be considered as having fixed employment. _ Engagements of servants may be made for 7. a month, half a year or a whole year. Servants, hired by half the year or the whole year shall only, at fixed periods, twice a year, on the 1st of April and the 1st of October, quit service, and those, hired by the month, only on the first day of every month. Unless otherwise agreed upon by the parties, notice to quit service shall be given by the master as well as by the servant at least one month before either of the aforementioned regular periods, if the servant is hired by the half year or the whole year, and at least 15

3 T © © I :& AT13, days before the end of the month, if he or she is engaged by the month. If no such notice has been given at the regular time, the contract shall be considered as having been renewed lor the term of service previously agreed upon. 8. The police court may, at the request of either the master or the servant, annul the engagement before or after the parly has entered upon service, if the demand to this etleci be founded on valid and equitable grounds, as for instance the incapability of the servant to perform the work agreed upon, non-attendance on his or her part, disobedience, immorality or other vicious conduct, ill treatment of cattle or domestic animals, if the servant has been guilty of leaving the house, or of allowing strangers to remain in the same during the night, without the consent of the master ; if the master abuses his authority or the right of chastising the servant, warranted to him by the provision of the Danish Code, 6-5-5 and 6, if he does not give the servant the necessary lood or lodging, and these defects are not remedied after a previous complaint to the Police Magistrate, on the subject, and a warning to the master, on the part of that functionary. Whenever a contract is annulled by judgment, on account of non-compliance on the part of the servant, he or she has no right to claim more than the wages already earned at the time ; and in such cases as well as in those in which the contract is annulled on account of abuse, on the part of the master, the guilty party

may, according to the circumstances, be adjudged to pay equitable damages to the other party, wntch, however, ordinarily shall not exceed the amount of three þÿmonths wages, if the servant is hired by half the year or the whole year ; and one month's wages, if he or she is engaged by the month. With regard to the infliction of punishment in such cases, the following general provisions will he applied, and the concerned may, moreover, according to the nature of the case, be adjudged to pnv damages, whenever one of the parties lias suffered any particular loss by the conduct of the other. $ 9 The master may. at any time, discharge a servant, bv paving to him or her. besides the wages already doe, one month's wages, if the servant is hired by the month, and three þÿmonths wages, if he or she is engaged for a longer term. The servant may likewise although hired by half the year or the whole year, demand without assigning any reason his or her discharge before the expiration of the term of service agreed upon, by paying three þÿmonths wages. Put the servant shall in such case notify his or her intention 4 weeks previously. 10. Any servant, having been engaged under a certain general denomination f: i: as coachman, cook or house-servant, may be employed bv the master in any other work, that may occur and which, according to common practice, may be reasonably required from such a servant. If the servant asserts to be expressly exempted from perlorming work of one kind or another, he or she must satis-

factorily prove the truth of such assertion. II. In case of sickness, which has not been caused by the þÿservant own s fault, the master is in duty hound to provide for the support of the servant residing with him, until he or she in consequence of notice given to this effect, or on any other legal ground, ought to quit service, but the wages shall cease from the time the servant has been unable to do his work, unless he or she, with the consent of the master, puts some other person in his or her place. The expenses for the cure of a sick servant, for medicine and such special tending as may be required, shall be defrayed by the servant. 12. The master is, for abuse of his authority or for non-performance of the duties incumbent on him, liable to a fine, according to circumstances, unless he has been guilty of such

conduct, as. according to laws in force, subjects him to a more severe punishment. For neglecting to make the report, preset tbed by 6, the master shall be liable to a fine of from half a dollar toikvc dollars. 13. Servants who out of the regular limes. or without any legal cause quit their service, are, at the request ol the master to be given warning by the police to return, and are, moreover, to be punished with an adequate fine and damages to the master, but if such a servant should quit anew his service or should refuse to return, after having received warning to this effect, he or she shall be punished with confinement on bread and water until 8 times 48 hours or with a corresponding imprisonment with hard labor where such is deemed proper and shall moreover, have forfeited to the master one þÿmonth s wages, if hired by the month, and three months' wages, if engaged for a longer term. For other transgressions or for neglect of their duties servants are liable to fines or to a more severe punishment, if the case should require such, and are, moreover to be adjudged to repair the loss caused to the master by their conduct. Neglect or improper conduct with regard to the serving-books shall be punishable with fines, or if attended with fraud, with a more severe punishment, and should it be necessary to procure a new serving-book, the value of the same shall be paid by the servant. 14.' The police courts have cognizance of all cases regarding the relations between masters
and servants.

As the day of the Election approaches the agonies of the þÿ þÿQuashers increase. Their cries have swelled from a groan to a howl. When the þÿ league was formed there was yet something approaching to an external show of decency, notwithstanding their tergiversations. The þÿ man of the þÿpeople manifested their machinations by publicly declining þÿ the honor of being elected and afterwards tacitly accepted, for the purpose of refusing ! If consistency did not demand, that he should not swerve from his expressed resolution, self-respect certainly required, that he ought not to have connived at the impositions of his confederates on the unsuspecting voters. When men cease to respect themselves they must expect, that nobody will respect them. The þÿQuashers at the outset þÿ acted in secret ; they were ashamed of exposing their play. But now every shadow of grace has vanished ; they publicly, hut in vain, appeal to the self-respecting constituents, depending in their despair on the powerful influence of the greut Agitator, whose veridical language they echo. Their fears have paralyzed every faculty except their utterance; and their howl is hideous. þÿ Save þÿus, cry they, þÿ from the pernicious results of an united þÿCouncil. þÿ We are willing to come to your assistance, respond the þÿ liberals, but will you go to the assembly and there advocate a disunion of council ? þÿ þÿ No þÿ! reply the former. þÿ Humbug, say the latter. The few passages at arms we had in our days have not rendered us callous

to the sufferings of our fellow-men ; we shall, therefore, sprinkle a few drops of cold reason on them to allay the heat. We beg most seriously to assure our friends þÿ the þÿQuashcrs, that we respect the opinion of every man, although it may he diametrically opposite to ours. Wc do not censure them for desiring þÿ a disunion of Council but we object to the method which they have adopted.

Diversity of opinion is to be expected on every subject. But decorum, policy, and common sense direct, that we should use loyal means to attain noble ends. , If they be in reality desirous of realizing their views, they certainly ought not to decline going to the Assembly. It is not by not acting that men in general obtain what they most desire. No, it is by doinjr. He who absents himself is in the wrong. Setting up candidates, who, when elected, will not accept the nomination is puerile ; it is besides a snare which will entrap only the unwary. Admitting, however, that our friends, the Quash þÿ þÿers succeed in their intention, which we doubt, of what avail will it e? Will it prevent the opening of the session, which no doubt will take place in October next ? Certainly not. According to the 25 of the Colonial Law, ten members form a working majority. Now, as j there are 13 members who have accepted their nominations, and the Government will appoint its 4 members, it is evident, that the non-election of the other three members for our Island cannot impede the proceedings of the Assembly. As these lines, however, cannot meet the eyes of the þÿ Quashers until alter the election, which we will not fail to make the subject of our next article, we will refrain till then from entering further in the details connected with the present question. The system of propulsion adopted by Captain Ericsson, and the engines constructed by him, have lately attracted so much attention that an abridged account, taken from an able article in the New York Merþÿchants Magazine, will be read with interest. Two engines upon this plan are now in operation at the works of Messrs. Within these are pistons exactly fitting each cylinder, and so connected that those in the lower and upper cylinders move together. A fire is placed under the bottom of each of the large cylinders, called the þÿ þÿ working þÿcylinders, those above being termed the supply þÿcylinders. As the piston in the supply cylinder moves down, valves, at the top admit the air; as it rises these valves are closed, and the air passes into a receiver and regenerator, where it is heated to about 450 deg., and, upon entering the working cylinder, it is further heated by the fire underneath. Eternity. þÿ What is this life but a circulation of little mean actions ! we lie down and rise again, dress and undress, feed and wax hungry, work or play, and are weary, and then we lie down again, and the circle returns. We spend the day in trifles, and when the night comes we throw ourselves into the bed of folly, amongst dreams, and broken thoughts, and wild imaginations. Our reason lies asleep by us, and we are for the time as arrant brutes as those that sleep in the stalls, or in the field. Are not the capacities of man higher than these and ought not his ambition and expectations to be greater? Let us be adventurers for another world. It is at least a fair and noble chance ; and there is nothing in this worth our thoughts or our passions. If we should lie disappointed, we are still no worse than the rest of our fellowmortals ; and, if we succeed in our expectations, we are eternally happy.

Always Busy. þÿ The more a man accomplishes the more he may. An active tool never grows rusty. You always find those men who are the mogt forward to do good, or to improve the times and manners, always busy. Who starts our railroads, our steam-boats, our machine-shops, and our manufactories? It is just so with a man who is benevolent þÿ the more he gives, the more he feels to like giving. We go for activity þÿ in body, in mind, in every thing. Let the gold grow not dim, nor the thoughts become stale. Keep all things in motion. We should rather that death should find us sealing a mountain than sinking in a mire þÿ breasting a whirlpool than sneaking from a cloud.

Our readers will learn from the following extract, that the architect of the well-known Tivoli and the Casino of Copenhagen, G. Carstensen, Esq., who very recently left this Islandfor America, is now, together with an eminent architect, joint builder of the New York Crystal Palace. From the Courier and Enquirer. The New York Crystal Palace, in which the American Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations is to take place, is to be opened to the public in May, 1853. The ground is to be broken for the foundation on Wednesday (Sept. 1), and the building will be pushed vigorously. The plan adopted is that furnished by Messrs. Carstensen and Gildemeister, the former of whom is the architect of the Tivoli and the Casino of Copenhagen; the latter has, some years since, achieved here an honorable repution in his profession. It is to be built entirely of iron and glass, and is to cost one hundred and ninety-five thousand dollars. It is difficult to describe

such a building so that (lie reader unlearned in architectural terms will obtain a just idea of its appearance; but the effect of the plan is more that of a can compare it to þÿ glass cathedral than save anything else we that the dome and pinnacles are surmounted with flags instead of crosses and statues of saints. Destructive Earthquake in St. Jago dc Cuba ! ! ! Commercial Circular received here : þÿ L' We translate from the Guadeloupe The following is a translation from a þÿ On the 20th instant (August), at 8 a. m., this city and its neighbourhood was exposed to a severe Earthquake, followed by successive shocks, which continued until the morning of the 24th. The inhabitants have suffered considerably ; there are few houses uninjured, the greater portion being in ruins. The cathedral, churches, and hospitals, and other public edifices, have been pronounced by a commission appointed to report upon them to be in the worse state. The country towns are also sufferers. During the period of four days the cities were deserted, and the inhabitants fled for safety in the country, and on board of the vessels in port. We have the pleasure to state that the greatest order prevailed ; there has been no robbery, and the public mind is about being restored to its usual tranquillity, owing to the impression that the commercial interest will not be materially affected, and it is expected that it will pursue its ordinary course, in nowise affected by this calamity ; þÿ all of which is due, in a great measure, to the activity of the Governor, and the different Authorities, who have exhibited on this occasion the greatest presence of mind and zeal. It is affirmed by many persons that comparing the Earthquake ofGuarieo and Pointe-a-Pitre in J842, those could not have been more severe than
the one experienced here, þÿaltho we find that we have to lament the loss of but seven lives. A great number of animals also perished.

þÿ this night will our souls be required of þÿus. The French Islands : Avenir, of the 28th ultimo, the following correspondence from the Governor of Barbados, to the Admiral commanding at Martinique, on the manufacture of Sugar by Doctor þÿStolle process: s þÿ þÿ Barbados, 5th August, 1852. þÿ Monsieur le Gouverneur, þÿ I have had the honor of receiving your þÿExcellency letter s of the 4th July, in which you express the desire to know if a substance known under the name of þÿ Arcanum has been used in this colony to manufacture sugar, and what may have been the result. I have sought such informations relative to the subject from persons who have made use of that composition in the management of the juice from the cane for the manufacture of Sugar, and have the honor to forward to your Excellency the replies given to me. I have also procured of Messrs. Cavan &. Co., of this Island, a box containing 20 canisters of the substance prepared by Doctor Stolle, and send them by this opportunity to your Excellency together with the invoice. The article is costly, but it remains optional to your Excellency to return the þÿ þÿArcanum, if it is found that it does not meet the views of the inhabitants or planters of Martinique. I avail myself of this opportunity to offer to your Excellency the expressions of my highest regard, with the assurance of the pleasure which I will always feel in being useful to you. I have the honor to be, Your þÿExcellency s Most humble and obdt. servt.. (signed) K. B. þÿHAMILTON.

Letter of Mr. II. I jtuis Young, to Mr. James Walker, Colonial Secretary in Barbados Marchfield, 31st Julv, 1852. My dear þÿSir The experiments made by me of Doctor þÿStolle composition s in the manufacture of sugar have been within a very confined limit, but such as they are 1 cheerfully communicate the same to your Excellency. Doctor þÿStolle process, s for the manufacture of sugar, has been used þÿ the liquor clarified, evaporated, and boiled to sugar in open copper pans. The use of the composition did not alter the necessity for making use of the same quantity of lime to clarify the liquor þÿ the result being a very bright color and clear. The liquor rejected little or scarcely any scum during the process of crystalization, although it was partially clarified whilst being poured into the coolers ; nevertheless it did not appear to be superior in quality to that made without the said composition. The sugar manufactured by this process, appears to have gained in quantity, because it is no more necessary to make a frequent use of the skimmer (palette), a process which removes, with the scum, a large quantity of liquor. I imagine the process liable to improvements, and that advantageous results would be obtained therefrom, by making use of vacuum pans, and the boilers of Godesden. 1 am, &c., (signed) H. LEWIS YOUNG.

Letter of Mr. Sambury, to Mr. James Walker, Colonial Secretary, Barbados: Estate Lovvthers, 31st July, 1852. 1 only received yesterday your letter of the 29th instant. Please inform His Excellency that I manufactured 12 hogsheads of sugar with liquor prepared hy the process of Doctor Stolle (Arcanum.) There is no doubt that this agent is an active clarifyer, which gives to the liquor a bright and handsome color; but I have found that the sugar, although apparently more handsome whilst in the coolers than the sugar manufactured by the ordinary process, becomes softer and damp when packed up in casks, a defect which I attribute to the existence, perhaps in the mixture of some saline matter. 1 have emptied a cask of sugar manufactured by means of this composition, and in the whole of the contents, found the sugar damp, notwithstanding its having been placed on stilts to facilitate its draining. At the end of the crop, our canes being in a very bad condition, we found it difficult to obtain sugar, but having a few pounds of the substance, I used it to clarify some liquor of a very bad quality, and the sugar produced proved far superior in quality to that manufactured from bad liquor, and without the aid of the þÿ Arcanum." 1 will reply with pleasure to all questions which may in future be addressed to me on this point. I am, Ac., (Signed) L. SAMBUIlY.

Settlement of the þÿFisheries Dispute. Our readers will be glad to learn, on the authority of the evening organ of the Government, that the þÿfisheries dispute with the American Union has been i brought to an amicable termination. At ! this every one must rejoice ; but the British colonists, for whose especial benefit this rupture with the United States was sought, and on whose account we sent armed vessels to the scene of the trespass, will be surprised to learn that the affair has been settled by our surrender of rights, the legality of which was not disputed by either of the contracting parties, and the infraction of which formed the ground of our interference. Certainly, this is a very ridiculous affair, the only gratifying feature of which is that a question has been set for ever at rest which ought not to have been mooted. It is not the concession which our Government has made to the Americans which is annoying, but the ridiculous figure which we cut in the eyes of the world, and more especially in the eyes of the Americans, by ending in conceding what we commenced in bluster to maintain. This is very humiliating to the national character, and very degrading to the executive power; but as we have been placed in this position by our present precious Ministry, we must submit to it with what grace we can command. The negotiation, it seems, which has thus amicably terminated, has been conducted in London, and the future historian of the Derby Ministry will not fail

to dwell on the circular letter which Sir John Pakington recently addressed to the governors of the American colonies, setting forth their rights, followed in a few weeks after by the capitulation which we are now assured has taken place. Conducted as this negotiation has been under the eyes of the First Minister of the Crown, it would be difficult to lind any parallel to it in modern diplomacy, marked as it has been throughout by such thorough bungling. If public opinion in this country is not not quite, impossible. The þÿPresident s positively extinct, and if the least sense þÿ of decency or spirit is to be found in the new Parliament, this absurd þÿfisheries

business will form the first reckoning to which the Ministry will be called. If we had let matters remain as they stood, we should have acted prudently, but the first move we take upsets the position behind which we had entrenched ourselves, and makes our vapouring ns harmless as the smoke emitted from the chimnies of the steamers which we sent to the waters of North America to protect the privileges of our fishermen. But it is some comfort to know that for the future all disputes about bays and headlands will be avoided, and that three miles from the shore are the limits sacred to the British colonists. Simplicity is always a virtue, and the persons who now rule the destinies of England are evidently adepts in it.
