The late Election. The demand for the Ballot has received an immense impetus arising out of the results of ihe last election. On all hands the evil of open voting is now openly acknowledged byall but those wliohavesome sinister object in coercing the conscience ofthe voter. With every succeedingelection the horrors of the present system are brought out in still stronger and more hateful relief, and, without this necessary protection to the man who desires to exercise his electoral privilege honestly, and in accordance with his own innate convictions, people who are not thoroughly independent will regard a popular system of representation as the greatest curse that can afflict a country. This is a lamentable state of things ; but it is in perfect accordance with the artificial state of society which exists at the present day, with the great interests which are always trembling in the scales at a general election, and with the unprincipled conduct which wealthy and ambitious men deem it necessary to pursue for the furtherance of their own peculiar þÿview s, or the aggrandisement of their own class. It is clear that, when men record a vote not in conformity with their own sentiments, and against a candidate whom they deem the most eligible to represent them in the House of Commons, the act is a fraud on their own convictions, a fraud on society, and destructive to the institutions under which we live. And yet how general is the rule þÿ how rare the exceptions ! In the small boroughs and cities

of the empire we either see corruption or intimidation practised, þÿ the voter is either bought by the candidate who offers the highest price, or influences are brought to bear upon him which he dares not disregard. In the counties the voters, for the most part, are the mere creatures of the landlords, to offend whom would be ruin. Look at Ireland. The scenes which occurred at the last election are the offspring of this unnatural system of popular election. Between the priest and the owner ofthe soil the wretched man has no choice. If he escape Scylla, he is lost in Charybdis. An object ofdeeper commisseration than the Irish voter þÿ tormented by his landlord, and threatened with eternal ruin by his spiritual adviser þÿ can hardly be imagined. The cruel, the helpless, and the degrading position in which the Legislature places the majority of Irish, as well as of English voters, renders the franchise a positive evil, and another Parliament will hardly be allowed to pass away without a remedy being found, and that remedy must be the Ballot. The only argument against giving the voter the power of exercising his own free choice at an election is, that it is un-EngJish. This hacknied apology is simply disgusting. Is it not still more un-English to bribe, to treat, to intimidate, and to ruin ? The Times, a week or two before the dissolution, estimated the cost of a general election at three millions sterling. For what purpose can this enormous amount of money be required ? Certainly not for an honest pur-

pose. The legitimate expenses of a contest are trifling; and, as a general rule, it may be stated that the smaller the constituency the greater the Sir Henry þÿWard s electioneering expenses at St. Albans cost him, we see it | Cotton on Plantation stated, upwards of £2000; his expenses I year at Sheffield about £160. But even in

defy corruption, there is a vast amount mily, of demoralisation. In this respect, the newly enfranchised towns are patterns of purity as compared with the old rotten places of considerable population, accustomed during centuries to return

"' 1 il, I þÿ I. <o at «> Jt st ATjSt members to Parliament. In such towns as Leeds, Birmingham, Manchester, and the other great places enfranchised by the Reform Bill, and where the treating and bribery have never yet been systematically introduced, a þÿcandidate s expenses are inconsiderable as contrasted with Shrewsbury, Bristol, Liverpool, and the old towns and cities. In this place the proofs of direct bribery and treating at the last election are plentiful as blackberries. Stringent as the new law is, the direct corruption was widespread. It was determined to buy the contest at all hazards, and it was well known previously who where and who where not accessible to a bribe. At no election since 1830 was half so much money spent by the Tory party here. To talk ofthe Ballot being un-English, when public morality is thus sapped and undermined on all sides by the existing system, is a liberty taken with truth which argues no inconsiderable powers ol lace on the part of those who put it forth. The main objectors to the ballot are those who fear the introduction of a better and purer system. A more hypocritical pretence than that secret voting is un-English or unmanly was never advanced in favour ol a rotten and corrupt system, which degrades the elector, and ostracises every candidate who relies on his personal merit, and scorns to stain his fingers by a dirty act. The ballot is, par excellence , the prerogative of the higher classes. They introduce it into their clubs, and exact it in its rigidity. Is it not as un-English at the Carlton as

at the polling booths of a country, a city,' or a borough? But then it is said that the non-electors have a right to know how the electors vote. Indeed ! This tenderness, this wolf-like sympathy for the non-electors is very amusing, an- þÿ other proof of the dishonesty ofthe objectors. Why not enfranchise the nonelectors? The remedy is very simple. A man is only accountable to his own conscience for his vote, and no person has a right to control him, even morally, in its exercise. Public opinion cannot fail to be concentrated on this great question until a remedy is provided. The doings which will be brought to light by the election committees will open the eyes of every man who is not wilfully blind to the infamy of the existing system. The Frails have not been confined to Shrewsbury and Derby. It will then be found that a wide spread system of debauchery has covered the land like net-work, and in its meshes will be caught many who have hitherto seemed virtuous and pure, þÿ pious persons, who with uplifted hands deprecate the ballot because it is un-English, but would not hesitate to buy the bodies and souls of the wretches who would consent to bar- I ter both forþÿ a consideration. þÿ Wilmer i and Smith's Times.

Emigration from America. Examination of a Mr. John Wesley Harrison, a Gentleman of Colour, from South Carolina. At a meeting within Lady þÿMico Institution, s Hanover-Street, Kingston, Jamaica, on the evening of Wednesday, the 23rd June, 1852. Presentþÿ Mr. Harrison ; Messrs. William Wright, James Davidson, and W. Wemyss Anderson. From what part of the United States have you come, corruption. ' you resided on this island ? what was your occupation there; and how long have I came from South Carolina. I had a Rice and there. I have been upwards of a this island. What induced you to change your home ? I did so simply on account of the oppression under the large towns and cities, where the ex- i which I, in common with other free persons of colour, tent of the constituency would seem to j laboured in that country. I wished, for myself and faa country where my family could have a fair chance of advancement in life, which I knew they never could have in America. My family consisted of a wife, six sons, and one daughter. 1 brought them all with me to this island. What has been your occupation in this island ? Shortly after my arrival I purchased the property called Orange Park, in ths pariah of Saint David ft

is a coffee property and cattle pen. I now reside there with my family. Had this country, and the state of society in it, disappointed you or otherwise ? The country has realized my expectations in respect of the soil, the climate, the nature and value and variety of its productions, and the state of society in reference to persons of colour. The one only disappointment I have had has been the labouring population. They are indolent, and inefficient beyond anything I have ever seen. I have lost a great deal of money in attempting to carry on cultivation with them. Their mode of working appears to me unskilful, and their implements are bad. Will you explain this more particularly ? Their hoes appear too narrow and heavy for the work of clearing and weeding. They seem to think a certain amount of work sufficient for a day, and they will not go beyond it. What amount of labour will an American free coloured labourer, such as you have been accustomed to hire on your own plantation in America, or to see on other properities in that country, perform, in comparison with labourers of the same class in this island ? I admit that the ground may be somewhat harder to work in this island than in South Carolina. A man there will readily, and he commonly does, clean an acre a day, the vegetation being as rank there in summer as ii is here. But I could guarantee that such labourers as 1 have been accustomed to employ in America would perform four times the work per day of the la-

bourers in this island. Did joh ever see sugar cultivation in America, and would your remarks apply to such labourers cleaning canes ? I have seen sugar cultivation in South Carolina ; almost every planter there cultivates a portion of sugar. My remarks apply to such cleaning as is required on cane fields. An acre and a half of cleaning of canes per day is a common task for free labourers therp, as well as slaves, to perform. I have always lound free labourers less troublesome than slave. Are you of opinion that any considerable number of free coloured labourers of that class may be induced to come to this island, and engage themselves as labourers on the plantations ; and it so, on what terms, at what rate of wages, and on what service could they be engaged ? From what I know, and from my late letters from America, I am convinced that almost the whole coloured population is in search of a country. I have no doubt that a verv little would induce multitudes, who are now agricultural labourers, to come to this island, and engage themselves in the like occupation on our plantations. The usual term of an agricultural þÿlabourer ! wages there, is from 85 dollars to 120 dollars a year. If he get the latter sum, he is only found in a house, and not in maintenance. If he get only from 80 dollars to 85 dollars a year, he gets half a bushel of meal and 3 lbs. of bacon a week in addition, the value of which is about half a dollar. But for this rate of wages and allowance they engage by the year, and work six

days in the week, and from sunrise to sunset. I think it would be quite sufficient to induce them to move if they knew that such engagements could be got in this island. They are at present afraid to move, on account of the small, imperfect, and contradictory accounts they have of this country, and their dread of destitution in going to a strange place where they have no friends or people whom they know. My remarks apply chiefly to the agricultural population of North and South Carolina and Georgia. The climate in these States in the summer season (which is the working season), is similar to that of this island, and so are the productions. But more can be done here, as there is no winter. I have had however, within the last nine months, letters from many persons in the States of New York and .i'ensylvania, expressing their interest in this country, and their desire to come to it. But they have been excel dingly perplexed by contradictory accounts, some from people in this island, dissuading them from coming. I am decidedly of opinion, that it would be much lor their benefit to come here, and beneficial also for this island. Many would come at their own expense, and many could not do so but would engage to work out the expense of their passage. But it would be imprudent to let them have their passages paid. How could they best be addressed, whether by newspapers, or agency, and what sort of agency ? Newspapers they seldom see. I think agents ought to be sent with the invitation to them to come. þÿ Agents

of their own colour would be most readily listened to. Do you think any considerable number would corns over as agricultural settlers ? Very great numbers ofthat class would come. þÿ Many of them with capital. Some with no inconsiderable amount of capital, which they would invest readily in the purchase of land, i am looking now daily for the arrival of some of that class. (Signed) JOHN WLSLLY HARRISON. The above testimon) given in presence of J. Davidþÿson s William Wright, and William Wemyss Anderson. Mr. Harrison subsequently informed me that the free people of colour carefully respect the family relations, and that the system of concubinage, which prevails so extensively in this island, would by them be regarded as exceedingly disgracetul. The lateness of the hour prevented an extension of his examination to the important topic of their social condition. As to their predilections, he stated that these were much stronger in favour of the British Government and its institutions than their own, which had only oppressed them. (Signed) WM. From the New York Herald, September 2. The New York Crystal Palace. We have seen plans of the exterior and interior of the intended building for this exhibition, which have been prepared by Messrs. Carstensen andGildemeister, and which cut rather a fine appearance on paper; and we are told that in beauty of architecture, though not in size, it will surpass the late London Exhibition building, which, in form and construction, it will closely resemble, and will, like that building, be constructed of iron and glass. The building, which will be erected in Reservoir Square, will be in the form of a Greek cross, having a nave and transcept, with two galleries and comlartments lition building, and will be surmounted similar to the London Exliiby a dome over the point of intersection. The diameter of the cross will be 365 feet in length, and 14!) feet in breadth, and the height of the dome will be 130 feet. The ground floor will contain 111,000 square feet, and the galleries 62,000 square feet, and the estimated cost of the building is $195,000. Fountains, trees, and natural and artificial decorations will be profuse ; the roof will be surmounted with the flags of the various foreign nations; and the dome will be embellished with elaborately painted escutcheons of the different States of the Union. We arc informed that the arrangements and preparations are rapidly progressing and that many of the articles exhibited at the London Exhibition will be re-exhibited. The building will be forthwith commenced and is advertised

to be open on the 2nd May next, and thing is certain, promises to be a that creditable affair. One unless the proprietors beat the London Exhibition they will entail upon themselves more contempt than honor. They must remember that they have taken upon themselves an affair which may be regarded by foreign nations in the light to of a na- tional undertaking, and woe them if they fall short.

From narana. private correspondence. Havana, August 28, 1852. The Government Spies þÿ The way the suspected Persons were arrested þÿ Names of the Prisoners, lc. Sfc. My Dear Friend: þÿ I made a mistake when I informed you, in my last letter,

8 "JN SIKIItZ A V I 8 that the Spanish government had lost the threal of its researches in regard to the revolutionary plan of Vuelta Abajo. Now th a!; 1 have got more correct informatioi upon this affair, I will communicate it to you. I do nt know how it came to happen that a min, by the name of Rives, who is a con\ict, condemned for larceny to the city thain gang, was fully informed of every thing in connection with that plan, am in order to obtain the grace of the government, and redeem himself from his fate, asked the second in command ofthe chain gang to carry him before the Captain-General. That officer scornfully refused, at first, to comply with þÿRives request; but, as he insisted in his demand, and revealed to him the whole jlan of the patriots, the commander look him to the Governor. The wretch denounced to li is Excellency the names of all those whom he supposes to be implicated, giving at the same time an account of the names of the streets and numbers of the houses where every one of them resides. In consequence of this denunciation, the arrests were made of which I informed you in my last. On this ground, General Canedo gave full credit to þÿRives further disclosures in regard to the revolutionary scheme in Vuelta Abajo, where large stocks of firearms, Ac., had been previously sent to arm large numbers of men who were ready to rise against the government through all that country, in connection with a great many wealthy and respectable citizens of Havana. Governor Canedo then ordered Colonel Guillen,

(lately arrived from Spain) to Vuelta Abajo, in company with a police officer, Barredo, and a large body of troops, among whom was Rives, disguised as a soldier, to point out all those whom the infamous convict has accused of being implicated in the conspiracy. Colonel Guillen proceeded to arrest all those persons, among whom we find Don Juan Gonzalez, a wealthy and respectable planter, sixty years old, and Don Joaquin Maria Pinto, a lawyer. The means employed by Colonel Guillen are those becoming to the ferocious character of tiger like Spaniards. Entering by force the peaceful houses of every citizen, insulting and grossly abusing the innocent tenants either men or ladies, holding the most indecent language, and behaving as ruffians, the commander ordered the head ol the family to be brought to his presence and then submitted him to the severest and most inquisitorial examination, in regard to the object of his commission. Every witness thus examined, deposed in favorable terms in regard to Gonzalez, as being an honest, peaceful and virtuous citizen. But Col. Guillen would not go back to Havana without having þÿ discoveredthe leaders of the revolutionary þÿplot. The witness is then condemned to be shot. He is taken to the ground in front of the farm house, placed on a chair, four soldiers came out with loaded muskets, and while they aim at the breast of the terrified fellow, the commander addresses him in an awful tone, in order to obtain the desired disclosures. In other cases the witness

has been tied to a tree or to a post and a number of soldiers, armed with clubs and sticks approach the victim and threaten to beat him to death; the commander repeats his injunctions, to force him to denounce the conspirators. In regard to the slaves they are whipped to death if they do not confess everything that they are suspected to he acquainted with. Those who comply with the desire of the government, right or wrong, are richly rewarded, so far that a mulatto man, a slave of Don Juan Gonzalez, has now joined the ranks of her Catholic þÿMajesty army, s as a recompense for hi

having revealed that his owner is a patriot. The government and its hirelings of the press, have made a great fuss about the supposed discovery of the office and type of La Voz del Pueblo ; but this is no such thing. The fact is, that some patriots, wishing to mislead the government in the course of its researches on that account, undertook the continuance of the Cuban free paper, and for that purpose they made use of the type of the office where the paper El Almendares is printed. While engaged in this work, a spy of the Spanish government, by the name of Johns, succeeded in gaining their confidence, and they were soon betrayed and denounced to the Captain- General, who immediately ordered the arrest of the following persons, as accomplices of the deed : þÿ Don Eduardo Facciolo, Don Eduardo Uriol, Don Udetonso Estrada y Zenea, Don Eduardo Sariel, Don Felix Maria Cassard, Don Florentine de la Torre, Don Antonio Granado, Don Antonio Rubio, Don Antonio Palmer, Don N. Urquizo. A mulatto man and two others, whose names I have not been able to ascertain. Besides this, the miserable spy informed that a gentleman named Palma was the supporter of the paper, but could not state what was his Christian name nor his profession ; and, notwithstanding this, the Captain-General issued an order for the arrest of Senor Don Ramon de Palma, a distinguished member ofthe bar in this city, upon no other ground but his wearing the family name mentioned by that wretched traitor. Senor Palma is now confined in one of the

dungeons of the Cubana Castle. The Spanish Government has made up its mind to make it appear before the world, that these revolutionary movements have their origin in the low class of our people, and among some disaffected individuals, who have no influence with this community ; and therefore, the arrest of those respectable, wealthy, and high standing Cubans, who now lay in the death-shadowed cells ofthe Spanish dungeons, have been made under cover of the shades of night, so that no one may hear of their fate, until their disappearance will be noticed by their friends. My dear friend we are on the border of the abyss, or on the eve of our redemption. The Lord of þÿ cide of our fate. Adieu. Ibid., Sept. 5. Mercy will de-

U\ plosion ol' the Steamer Reinþÿdeer B s oiler. THE LATEST AND MOST AUTHENTIC PAR- TICULARS. Saugerties, Sept. 4 þÿ 6 P. M. The steamer Reindeer, Capt. Charles W. Farnham, left New York at eight þÿo clock this morning, and arrived at Malden, Saugerties landing, at a quarter after one o'clock p. m. She had landed the Saugerties passengers, and was drawing in her gang plank, when the pipe which connects the flues, called the connection ofthe return flues, burst. The steam rushed out between decks, tearing down a temporary bulk head and passing through a pantry into the lower cabin, where a number of passenger were dining.

The work of destruction in the dining cabin was complete, every person there being either killed or badly injured. The steam also passed up the chimney, carrying away the smoke pipe, which fell across the hurricane deck breaking it down. No persons, however, were injured above the deck, except the engineers and cooks. We have witnessed the scene of disaster, and a more heart-rending spectacle was never beheld. Language cannot describe the condition or appearance of the pitiable objects we saw. Our citizens are unremitting in their offices of kindness to the suffering, and their friends at a distance, may he assured that nothing will be omitted to render the wounded as comfortable as possible. þÿ Ibid.

Loss of flic Steamer Atlantic. Buffalo, August 20, 1 852. The steamer Atlantic came in collision with the propeller Ogdensburg, at two þÿo clockthis morning, and sunk in about half an hour. The loss of life from the Atlantic i3 estimated at two hundred persons þÿ while about a like number were taken on board the propeller, which was leaking badly ; but they succeeded in reaching Erie with her. A dense fog prevailed at the time of the collision. Immediately after the collision, which was very severe, the Utmost confusion prevailed amongst the steerage and deck passengers, a very large portion of whom , were Norwegian emigrants, and several, it is thought, in the terror and darkness that prevailed, jumped overboard at once. The passengers were all in bed, and the first mate was on duty. Captain þÿI etly,although seriously injured, with the assistance of the crew, endeavored to calm the fears of the passengers, assuring them there was no danger. The steamer kept on her course, the officers hoping to be able to reach port, although the boat was leaking badly ; the water, however, gained rapidly on them, despite the efforts of the crew, and by the time they had proceeded about two miles from the spot where the collision took place, it was found that the vessel was rapidly sinking, the fires in the engine room being extinguished by the water. The emigrants, who could not understand a word spoken to them, by their cries and terror added to the horror of the scene. The cabin passengers, and all who could be made

to understand, were exhorted by the captain and officers to remain in the cabin, and provide themselves with chairs, settees, beds, &c., all of which were patent life preservers, and would buoy them up in the water. Numbers, however, unheeding, and not understanding the advice given them, rushed overboard to certain death. At about half-past two þÿo clock, admidst the wild shrieks of the passengers, the steamer settled and sunk. The propeller had kept in the wake of the Atlantic, and those on board her did all in their power to preserve the lives of the hundreds of human beings who were now seen struggling in the water. The fog was a sad hindrance to their efforts, but some two hundred and fifty were rescued from the lake, and taken by the propeller to Erie. A large number left at once on the Sultana for Cleveland þÿ others came down in the cars this morning. From the best information we can gain, we are led to believe that some two hundred lives are lost. There is reason to hope that many may yet be saved on the life preservers, with which the boat was well fifrnished. All the passengers saved by the Ogdensburg had nothing on but their night clothes. Immediately on the news being received in this city the steamers Northern Indiana and I,ouisiana, and propeller þÿl rinceston, offered their services to go to the wreck. The Louisiana, which was fired up, immediately prepared to start; but the þÿcompany b s oat Cleveland arriving from up the Lake, was instantly despatched to the scene of the catastrophe. She saw

nothing of the wreck on her down trip, owing to the fog. The steamer Clayton has gone to the wreck from Erie. The emigrants were Norwegians, who came through, by Lake Ontario steamers, from Quebec, and about seventy-five or eighty of them were left on the dock, the agent refusing to suffer them to goon board. They now mourn the loss of their friends. An express company had about $50,000, in money, on board the boat The boat belonged to the Messrs. Wards, owners of the Caspian, lately lost at Cleveland. She was valued at $80,000 and was not insured. þÿ Ibid, August 21.

Asiatic Cholera. A correspondent þÿ of the North British Daily Mail writes as follows: þÿ þÿ Reasoning from what happened in 1835 and 1847, Asiatic cholera will, in the course a of few months, perhaps weeks, visit Glasgow for the third time, to sweep into the grave thousands of its citizens. 1 believe it would prove of material use towards the prevention of this fearful scourge, were it well understood by the public, that three factors seems necessary for its production. The
tution of the element, or an unknown agent present, with them, now, for the third time, moving steadily on from east to west, from Hindostan, through Persia, Turkey, Russia, Poland, and Prussia,

America and tfie West Indies. The second factor seems necessary to fix the first in its transit, and consists in the miasmata arising from putrifying animal and vegetable substances left exposed in the alleys and neglected receptacles for filth in over-crowded towns, and especially in those parts of them which are. illsupplied with water and incompletely drained. The third factor is a debilitated condition of the human body, brought on by the employment of improper articles of food, especially such as lead to looseness of the bowels, and by the habitual use of intoxicating drinks. The first of these factors has hitherto proved inscrutable in its nature, and has resisted all attempts to limit its progress by sanitary cordons or quarantine regulations; but the second and third are, in a great measure, within our own power, entirely indeed, were we to put in operation our protective means against them early enough ; and there can be little doubt that if either of them can be annihilated, the first factor would pass over us without mischief. Cleanliness, then, and temperance are the preventives of cholera; dirt and drink beckon it and welcome it to the scene of its destructive dealings with human þÿlife. OBITl'AltY. DIED-on Friday afternoon, the 22nd instant, of Fever, at the Parsonage, the Reverend John Wade, a. m., Rector of St. Paul's Church, Frederiksted. His remains were interred at the church on Saturday, attended hy a very large concourse of sorrowful friends, parishioners and citizens. Mr. Wade was horn in Ireland þÿ came to this Island in January 1850 þÿ was aged 44 þÿ and had been in the ministry 16 years.

On Sunday morning at St. John's, the Rector, addressed the congregation in the following words: þÿ Dear Brethren, þÿ The stern "king of terror's" death is very busy all around us; yea, in our very midst, teaching and " en- forcing the impressive lesson, that in the midst of life we are in death." Another worthy Brother and zealous co-laborer in the ministry has fallen beneath his relentless stroke and entered into rest. It is very difficult even for the minds of those of us, who have been to the house of mourning and even assisted at the burial, to realise the startling fact, that the Reverend Mr. Wade, who seemed so full of health and the promise of a long life, is dead : but even so it is ; his soul has passed into the spirit world þÿ ascended to God who gave it, and the grave has closed over his mortal body. We, Brethren, shall see hiin no more, till the resurrection of the just, llis memory and the fruits of his great services anil unreserved labors, alone remain to ns ; in these services and labors, you brethren, have participated. You can testify how promptly and faithfully he ministered to you for four months, without omitting any of the duties of bis own parish þÿ how unreservedly he gave himself and spent his great strength þÿ not in amassing wealth not to gain the perish- þÿ able, but to win souls to Christ. Equal zeal and self-devotion, combined with equal physical strength and energy are too seldom united. Scarcely a day passed that he was not visiting some part of his

parish and mingling with all classes of nis people. On the very day of the evening of the commencement of his sickness, he had been visiting a poor sick laborer on a distant estate and passed several hours there. He added to the morning service an evening service on Sunday, with an evening service during the week. But what has seemed to me a greater marvel, and often awakened my warm admiration of Mr. Wade, was the readiness and efficiency with which he adapted himself to the difficulties and peculiarities of a voluntary congregation. Educated under the auspices of a richly endowed church ; whose ministers are placed beyond dependancc on their people for support, and for many year's serving in that ministry þÿ he entered energetically upon what was emphatically the great difficulty of his parish þÿ a great difficulty in fact of all voluntary congregations, and carried it on with a success, that few, if any, who have been accustomed to the voluntary system could have surpassed, while we believe not one in a hundred of those brought up in an endowed church would have equalled. You must remember brethren, that God makes use of various instruments for the building up of his kingdom on earth and none of these are perfect. The zealous, resolute and stout-hearted Paul þÿ the imftetuous oving, lamb-like John. Each with in- and impatient Peter þÿ the mild, firmities peculiar to himself and incident to human nature. To say that our departed Brother may not have had infir-
mities would be to exalt him from a man and the infirmities of a man into the perfections of a God. He possessed in an

8 JN <© 1U 'fil 1 SL eminent degree some of the first requisites of an efficient minister þÿ firmness mingled with kindness þÿ a disregard of the world's opinion þÿ implying a strong and undouhting faith þÿ and an entire and u reserved consecration of his talents and great strength to the of souls to Christ. I fear it will be long before bis bereaved parish will find another Pastor to equal him in these virtues. But Brethren my heart is too full þÿ too sad indeed to do more this morning than pay this passing tribute þÿ I attempt no sketch of his life at present, I only ask dear Brethren, What mean these sad, these unusual deaths of the Pastors of your Church; a Mines, a Richards, a Wade þÿ Brother Ministers who seem but yesterday to have been standing in this pulpit wliere I now stand, have all been called home to that rest which remaineth for the people of God, in three consecutive months. I ask again Brethren, What mean these judgments beginning at the house of God? Are the righteous taken from the evil to come, and are we spared that we may endure more evil days, and more trying times ? Be it our's Brethren to humble ourselves in prayer and self abasement under the mighty hand of God, anil be still. In health and strength, (for in sickness we see, that we shall have no time) let us prepare to meet our God.

£3? We have been kindly favored, by a Member of the Colonial Council, with the following Pari of a Speech on the question of labor, given in the 3rd sitting of the Colonial Council in St. Croix, the 11th October 1S52.

Sir, I bog leave to call the attention of the Council to certain facts deserving notice. In a printed voucher which has been laid before us, a document equally remarkable for the thoroughness, the lucidity, and the truthfulness of its investigations, I find it stated that, during the first three years after the emancipation, at least 12 JO individuals of the laboring class have left the sugar estates in St. Croix. Another document laid before us shows that, on the 1st October 1851, the following numbers of laborers have left the sugar cultivation, viz. in St. Croix 267, in St. Thomas 39, in St. John 31. On the 1st October of the present year 1852 the sugar cultivation in St. Croix has sustained a further loss of 424 individuals of the laboring class, and I am informed that 70 and odd out of the number shipped themselves to the town of St. Thomas. Thus we see the labor, on which the welfare of these colonies depends, decreasing, continually decreasing, and decreasing to an extent which threatens with approaching ruin. The question arises, how is the evil to be remedied ? If this Council shall answer : " the laborers are free, you cannot prevent them from seeking their maintenance by other means than agriculture ; the decrease is an evil, certainly, but there is no remedy" þÿ then I say : our labors, just commenced, have been finished before commencing ; if we frame a hundred laws, the wisest on earth, it avails nought ; the most glorious seasons that Providence may grant avail nought ; a deadly cancer

is devouring the marrow of these islands, ruin is approaching, slowly perhaps, but sure, inevitable, there is no remedy. If the Council shall answer : surely, an evil " like this can be remedied, aud must and shall and will be remedied" þÿ then I say, in God's name, let us put hands to the work with a good heart, for we may hope. What is the task before us ? To establish that system of laws by which emancipation is to be carried out. Let us cheerfully and with energy apply ourselves to the task, trusting that, if we succeed, then, and only then, emancipation will be hailed as a true benefit to society, a great and good work performed in the service of humanity and civilisation. Then the many eyes that are now turned upon us may not meet with disappointment

What, then, is emancipation ? Some people are of opinion that it is a very easy thing, merely to pronounce slaves free, merely to put them in a condition of equality with other members of society, and leave matters to seek their own level. This has been the theory of the philanthropists of England, a theory tried by practical experience in the British colonies, now for a period of 18 years. The result of the experiment is known to the world. First you heard the general cry want of labor , then that of immigration , then again the former want of labor. Coolies are imported at a great expense ; the want seems supplied ; yet after a little while you still hear the same old complaint want of labor. What is the cause of the phenomenon ? Might you not suspect that the immigrated Coolies are contaminated by the emancipated natives ? Ought you not to doubt the soundness of the British system of emancipation ? In one of our islands you see the result of the system staring at you daily across the narrow channel, a palpable warning not to adopt anything similar. " emancipation is freedom there is reason to ex- of that system which is based on the sentence Accordingly, if you must doubt the soundness ," pect some mistake as to the meaning of this sentence. Emancipation is abolition of slavery, and thus far you may call it freedom. But nil fit per salturn in reruin natura , nature never leaps. Therefore emancipation, by the rule of nature, must introduce freedom, not all at once, but slowly, by

degrees, abiding time. Emancipation is the throwing down of the bar which separates slavery from freedom. That done, the task commences, of leading the emancipated generation on towards the goal of freedom. This task is a heavy one It cannot be performed in a day, nor by the stroke of a pen. In the annals of antiquity we find recorded an instance of emancipation, singularly illustrative of the task which is now before us. For centuries a nation of upwards of half a million lived in thraldom At last they were liberated. The goal held before them was the land of promise. But, after being liberated from thraldom, they were kept wandering in the desert for forty years, and wo learn that, while thus wandering, they were longing, not for the land of promise, but for the fleshpots of Pliarao. When all had died who had issued from thraldom, their children reached the land of promise. We may compare our emancipated laborers to the Jews ; for both were in thraldom, and were liberated. We may compare freedom to the land of promise ; for the one like the other was the goal held out to the liberated. We may, perhaps, compare that freedom which at present is the desire of our emancipated laborers, to the fleshpota of Egypt which were the objects of the longings of the wanderers in the desert ; for neither the one nor the other we find to answer the purpose of liberation. I do not wish to extend the comparison so, as to say, that, likewise as the J ews were wandering about in the desert, thus our 1&-

boreis should move about in these islands ; for in order to complete that comparison we should imagine these islands to become deserts. But I do wish, and I do hope, that a day may come when our present Colonial Government, to whom has been entrusted the care of leading our emancipated negroes on towards freedom, may truly be compared toþÿ MOSES, standing on the mountain, and from that elevated position viewing in the distance, far off in the distance , that land of promise, for the possession of which he had been laboring for forty years, and yet where he should never set his foot ; for thus it was ordained. But, whether our Colonial Government will be guided by that wisdom which guided Moses, and which surely was dipped from the very depths of the fountains of knowledge of mankind and human nature, or whether our Colonial Government þÿ will grasp impatiently at the goal, before the time is, and miss it þÿ remains to be seen. In this respect the Honorable Council present will stand responsible before posterity. We all feel it, when we are gone it will be judged, hrae we fulfilled our task. I have alluded to the earliest ( mancipation of the Jews. The land of promise was their freedom. It took them forty years to reach it. Denmark itself affords another instance of emancipation, carried out on the same principle In Denmark bondage existed until the last day of the former century. How was it' abolished ? History informs us that the abolition commenced more than a whole century before, if I remember
rightly in the year 1695, progressing gradually during subsequent years, until finally, by the Ordinance dated 20 June 1788, it was decreed that, from the 1st of January 1800 bondage should

cease to exist. But before that day arrived, several ordinances prepared the change it was to bring, by limiting that freedom which the abolition of bondage otherwise might carry along with it. Among these I shall only mention an Ordinance dated 25th March 1791, which imposed on the peasantry in Denmark the obligation of engaging themselves as servants or farm-laborers. This obligation was general ; the cases to which it was not made applicable were exceptions from the rule ; and the reasons on which the Ordinance has founded the measure we find stated to be : " in order to promote agriculture, maintain good manners, and prevent vagrancy and demoralisation and the like abuses.'1'' Thus, in Denmark, the personal liberty of the emancipated class was limited according to the demand of circumstances and habitudes there. The limits, defined by law, were allowed to remain intact until the year 1840, when they were partially removed or modified by an Ordinance dated 16th December ; and not until the 5th of June 1849, the birthday of the present Constitution of the realm, did the Danish peasant emerge into the full enjoyment of that liberty, the door to which was unbarred on the first day of our century. This was the emancipation in Denmark. To consummate it took a period of half a century. It has left Denmark powerful enough to resist her enemies, wealthy enough to make war with them and, after all, in a flourishing condition. Draw your conclusions. The calm voice of His-

tory warns us what to avoid, advises us what to follow. If emancipation is carried out here on the same principle as it has been in Denmark, the result may finally turn out beneficial to these Islands. That cannot be done by introducing here the same system of labor as in Denmark. Circumstances are too widely different. In Denmark steady and continuous labour is the earnest wish and desire of the laboring class, and therefore the public welfare, as far as it depends on labor, rests secure. With us steady and continuous labor is, I might almost say, the aversion of our laborers. This antipathy may be a natural consequence of not yet forgotten slavery ; but, whether natural or not, it is there. Hence public welfare with us, as far as it depends on labor, has no secure foundation. Our system of labor, therefore, must be different from that of Denmark, yet based on the same principle ; that is to say, in order to promote agriculture, maintain good manners, and prevent vagrancy and demoralisation and the like abuses, the extent of the personal liberty of the laboring class must be regulated according to the demand cf our circumstances and habitudes here. How has this been done hitherto ? Y ou havo instituted contracts by the year, and fixed the amount of wages by law, pleading that these limitations of liberty are demanded by the public welfare, and that they have hitherto saved us from ruin. Be it so ; our Islands are not yet ruined. But, whoever will open his eyes and see, must be

aware that these limitations of liberty with regard to contracts of labor have merely retarded ruin. They prevent us from plunging into ruin all at once, but at the same time allow ruin to advance one great pace every year. This system is deficient. It protects the welfare during the term of the contract, and at the expiration of the term leaves it to take care of itself. Two things stand opposite each other. Onono hand welfare dependant on continuous labor. On the other a decided unwillingness with the laborers to undertake continuous work. Here lies the root of the evil to be obviated. That unwillingness can only be conquered in course of time. But, while it lasts, it evidently cannot be considered safe, that the movements of the laborers, who are unable themselves to foresee the consequences, shall be directed merely by the strength of their present antipathies. This must unavoidably jeopardise the general welfare. In St. Croix agriculture has lost, since the emancipation, upwards of 2000 laborers. By the continuance of this system, one estate after another must drop out of cultivation, as it were by accident, for it depends almost entirely on the whim or caprice of the laborers ; the towns are filled with idlers, and some few large estates with a superabundance of pretended laborers, of whom a great number are allowed to live there without working, or working at their own leisure ; at last the system, having reduced cultivation within bounds sufficiently narrow, breaks down itself.

This is, at present, the actual state of matters, and the end it must come to, if the system bo not modified so as to shape a different course. The remedy must obviate the cause of the evil, viz. the disposition of the laboring class to avoid continuous labor

3 T 0 & II ATI! 3. You will, perhaps, tell me that the Vagrant Law affords this remedy. But I think it does not. The Vagrant-Law applies only to cases of vagrancy when they are already at hand. Now, if the system is good, such cases will be comparatively few, and the Vagrant-Law will be, what it ought to be, a supplement to the system. But, as it is now, the system itself brings cases of vagrancy into existence, and supplies the Vagrant-Law with such overwhelming numbers of cases for its application, that vagrancy, instead of being a mere exceptional phenomenon iu our society, becomes a habitual one. The system, as it is now, promotes vagrancy ; the Vagrant-Law retrenches vagrancy. Thus the two work against each other, and work confusion. My opinion is, they must both work together the same way ; the system must prevent vagrancy, and the Vagrant-Law retrench vagrancy when, notwithstanding, it happens to occur. To demand, or even to expect, more from a Vagrant-Law is, in my opinion, an essential error. The system, then, must obviate the disposition of the laborers to direct their movements so as to avoid continuous labor. To this effect the system ought on the one hand to vindicate the natural right of the laborer to gain his maintenance by what sort of honest labor he is able, on the other hand provide means to prevent the abuse of this right when exercised merely to avoid continuous labor. In other words, the law must not leave the movements of the laborers to be directed only by the power of their own decided unwillingness

to work, but enable Government to prevent such movements as take place for no other purpose than to avoid labor. Thus, I repeat, as long as the disposition to avoid labor is predominant with the laboring class, their movements cannot safely be left to the guidance of this disposition, and it becomes imperiously necessary that Government, through the appointed authorities, must guide the movements, so that these may lend to improve the condition of the individual laborers, and not to destroy the welfare of our colonies. Let the authorities be disinterested, impartial men, dutiful towards the true interests of our society, and you need not hesitate to entrust them with this guidance, which you cannot do without, nor give into better hands.' If the philanthropists say that our emancipated people are still unfree, heed them not, but trust that your philanthropy is sounder than theirs. Their mission is to give the impulse to great acts of humanity, such as the British emancipation in 1834. In this respect they are like the steampower of civilisation, requiring to be directed bf proper machinery. If the steam is no longer controlled by the machinery, destruction ensues. The laws are the machinery, and no enthusiast can be a legislator. It is written that Government is from God. And why ? because Government shall guide and protect and take care of the minors and those who cannot guide and protect and take eare of say to the minors : " look here, you love free- themselves. Therefore, if Government should

dom ! well, we give you freedom to guide and protect and take care of " yourselves" þÿ might answer, perhaps, thank you Massa, God the minors bless you Massa" þÿ but I say, the Massa would not deserve the blessing, for he had mocked the duty which God laid upon his shoulders. After all Liberty, glorious Liberty, is but one of the qualified good things of this world. Likewise as you will not peal off the skin of your head in order to make it fit the hat of Liberty, thus you shall not sacrifice the welfare of society in order to introduce Liberty. Welfare be our standard, and Liberty will follow, in due time, when it will not endanger, but ensure our welfare.

Willmer and Smith' s European Times, October 1, 1852. The Late Duke of Wellington. The body of the Duke still remains at Walmer Castle, and has been placed in a leaden coffin, supplied by Messrs. Dowbiggin, Holland and Co., to whom the more urgent arrangements of this kind were entrusted. The outer coffin, which is of mahogany, is also ready, and waiting only for the inscription, which, of course, must now he decided on by higher than family authority. A second inscription is also, it is understood, to be inserted in the leaden coffin. It is said that the features have been little changed in expression by the hand of death, a circumstance the less surprising from their singularly marked character. Mr. Adams, an artist whose name Swill he remembered as the successful competitor for the design of the jurors' medal in the Great Exhibition, has been fortunate enough to secure a cast of the Duke's face, and this memorial will, no doubt, hereafter be highly valued as an authentic likeness. The funeral will he postponed until after the meeting of Parliament, in the month of November, by which time the arrangements will have attained such a point as will secure for it a thoroughly national and imperial character. The body ot the Duke will remain at Walm er till the period that may he fixed tor the lying in state, and in the meantime probably be temporarily deposited in a vault at the castle. With regard to the funeral, it is not at all unlikely, since the ceremony is to be thus delayed, that the initiative in the matter may he taken by the two

Houses moving an address to her Majesty, humbly requesting that a public funeral may be awarded to the departed hero. Such a course would, perhaps, add a more imposing and national character to the ceremony, as causing it to emanate from the three estates of the realm, instead of making it depend upon the authority of the Sovereign alone. In that case, it is obvious that no programme will he published, nor will any public step he taken till Parliament shall have met, and formally sanctioned, by a joint address, a course in which it has already been anticipated by the voice of the entire nation. 1 he Duke has lei t two sons. þÿ Arthur, Marquis of Douro, now Duke of Wellington, born 3rd February, 1807, and married to the daughter of the Marquis of Tweedalc, but has no issue, and Lord Charles Welleslcy, married to Miss Pierrepoint, by whom he has a young family. The whole Prussian army is ordered to wear mourning for three days for the Duke of Wellington. A deputation of Prussian officers will probably proceed to I.ondon to attend the funeral of their late and only field-marshal.

The New Commander-in-Chief. Lord Hardinge was born in 1785. He entered the army in 1801, and served with great distinction in Spain and Portugal. He was also at Waterloo, and lost his left hand, for which he receives a pension. He was Governor-General of India from April, 1844, to January, 1848, and he was present as Governor- General, and was second in command, at the battles on the Sutlej, December, 1845, and January, 1846. For his services on these occasions he received the thanks of Parliament, and was raised to the peerage. He also received the llianks of the East India Company, the freedom of the city of London, an annuity of £5000 lrom the East India Company for his own life, and a pension of £3000 from Parliament for the lives of the next two successors in the peerage.

We extract fiom the St. Thomas Times of the '27th instant the following copy of a letter To the Director of the Itoyal Rail Meant Packet Company. Gentlemen ! The repeated complaints which, from time to time, for some years past, have appeared in the public journals of the treatment of passengers by the West India Steamers, have to tbe present time bad no effect in bringing about the removal of the grievances complained of. Tbe utmost indifference and callousness have been shown by tbe Company to the continuous calls for reform : vessel after vessel is despatched from Southampton, overloaded with cargo, þÿ the space intended, and which should be reserved for passengers being occupied with goods on freight

The many complaints on these points having induced no improvement, it is almost hopeless to expect that another appeal will have the effect of securing the necessary precaution for the safety and comfort of passengers, still we think that we should not separate without making public our very strong disapprobation at the state in which the Royal Mail Ship Medway þÿ by which we were passengers þÿ was sent to sea, þÿ the more so that immediately before starting from Southampton three of the Directors of the Company, besides the Superintendent, were on board, and must have been aware of the overloaded state in which she was, and of her inability to make the passage with anything like comfort, and perhaps safety to passengers. The Medway sailed from Southampton on the afternoon on the 2nd instant, with upwards of one hundred passengers, exclusive of children, in a state of confusion indescribable. The space on the main-deck, intended for the resort of passengers in bad weather (with exception of a narrow passage fore and aft, and to the spar-deck), blocked up with cargo on freight, so that in the heavy weather with almost continuous rain experienced for eight days after departure, when remaining on deck was impracticable, the passengers were huddled up in a small space not allowing a sufficiency of standing room for each, without any convenience for sitting, or any possibility of moving about, in a manner barely equalled in a small and badly fitted out emigrant ship. A great part of the incumbrance, consisting of heavy

packages, was stowed immediately over part of the machinery, and from weighing down the deck might have been the cause of serious injury and risk to the safety of the ship. Below, on the forward deck, things were in the same position þÿ a bare passage being left, by the stowage of packages, to allow passengers having berths there to scramble to them as they best could. There is no question we think that the hampering up the main-deck of the ship with heavy cargo, and the stowage there and on the spar-deck of a large amount of heavy iron and wooden work belonging to the Company rendered her crank and top-heavy, and in some manner unfit to combat the heavy weather generally experienced in leaving Britain at this season of the year. And it is high time that some means were adopted to prevent more cargo being taken than can be stowed in the hold, nnd to have passengers' luggage placed in a baggage-room, where it will not he exposed on deck to damage as in the present case. As matters are now managed, the Commanders of the Royal Mail Company's Ships, we believe, are not allowed to interfere as to quantity or receipt of cargo, but are obliged to take the ships to sea in whatever state the Company see fit þÿ and, however willing they may he to make their passengers comfortable, it is often, as in the present case, out of their power. FRANCE. loth Sep. with repeated cries of " Vive PEmpe- Louis Napoleon was received at Nevers on the reur In answer to the Council-General of Nevers, who repeated their address in favour of the empire, the President said, when the general interest is at stake I try to anticipate public opinion, but I follow it in the case of an interest which may appear personal. The Prince President, since his departure on his provincial tour, has been everywhere saluted by acclamations of "Vive l'Empereur!" At Nevcrs M. Charles Dupin, in presenting to him the General Council of the Nievre, over which he presided during the last session, recalled the resolution adopted unanimously by the members in favour of stability of the Government, and he added, that the whole population had come to-day to give to this resolution unmistakeable sanction. The Prince, after thanking the Council for with these words : þÿ the manifestation of these sentiments, concluded " When it is the general interest that is in question, I always endeavour to anticipate public opinion ; but when it is an interest which appears to me to be personal, then I follow public opinion." This answer has produced a profound impression in Paris. No second opinion is entertained on the subject, and the restoration of the empire is universally looked on as a point settled in the mind of Louis Napoleon. The Austerlitz, line-of-battle ship, fitted with an auxiliary screw, has just been launched at Cherbourg ; and another screw line-of-battle-ship,

the Jean Bart, of 100 guns, has also been launched at Lorient. Mr. Guizot has arrived in Paris, but only intends to remain a short time. We learn, by telegraph, that, at Lyons, in inaugurating the Emperor Napoleon's statue, the of " Vive VEmpereur President delivered a speech alluding to the cries ." He said the same shouts which hailed the Emperor accompanied him (the President) throughout his present journey ; but the cry was a souvenir more touching to his heart than to his pride. His only aim was that of reconstituting in France a peace based on conciliation and principle ; and he declared that it was not from any personal interest lie would desire to change the modest title of President to that of Emperor. This speech was received with the most tumultuous applause. The negotiation with Belgium not having led to satisfactory results, the Moniteur publishes a decree, fixing the duty on coals imported by land in the zone comprised between Hallium and Longwy, at 30 centimes per " 100 kilograms. The duty on rough iron castings, fontes brutes," imported by land from Blancmisseron to Longwy, is fixed at 5f. per. 100 kilograms. On the 9th Sep. a brigade of gendarmerie sent by the government took possession of the mains of the chateau of Lepaud, belonging to the Orleans family. The person in charge of it protested against the act. A letter from Marseilles, of the 20th, states that the fireworks preparing for the fete for the Prince President were destroyed by the acciden-

tal explosion of a bomb. The roof of the worktered to pieces. Several persons were seriously injured. The director of the manufactory, M. shop was blown off', and the building nearly shat- _ Camoins, is not expected to survive. It is said that the Senate has resolved to go as far as Tours to meet the President, on his return to Paris in the middle of next mouth. The rnu- 'nicipal council of Paris is about to vote the President a solemn reception. Thus honours as groat as ever were bestowed on Charlemagne will

be conferred upon the author of the coup d'etat of December 2. The correspondent of the Morning Herald writes : þÿ The people of the south literally worship Napoleon ; the workmen, for finding continual employment ; the merchants, because they can carry on their business with security. They (the people of Marseilles) now have the near completion of the railroad to the Channel, the perspective of extensive docks, a new exchange, a cathedral, a splendid hospital, and many other important improvements. The clergy are attached to the Prince. This, too, in the south, hitherto the hotbed of legitimacy. SPAIN. This regulation takes effect as from September 2, the day on which official advices were received that Spanish ships would enjoy similar privileges in British ports. VENEZUELA. We are informed upon good authority that a new impulse has taken place in agriculture in Venezuela, as regards the production of sugar, steam power having been recently introduced lor grinding, instead of the old slow system of cattlemills, which is likely to develope the rich resources of that country, which have hitherto been lying comparatively dormant. About a year ago a small steam engine was put up on an estate, on the rich alluvial soil bordering on the lake of Va-

lencia, where water power could not be obtained, and which, until then, had been worked by mules, at a great expense and labour. This essay has proved so favourable that several of the neighbouring planters have been induced to follow it up ; and Mr. John Graham, an intelligent engineer, from Glasgow, who first imported the steam engine in question, was commissioned by several planters to return to this country, to procure four engines, varying from eight to twelve horse-power, and he is now on his way out to superintend their erection. Heretofore the production of sugar in Venezuela has been very limited ; indeed, very little more than the consumption of the country required; but with tlio«introduction of stenni to that country, we may soon expect a new source of supply of this valuable article of commerce, which, in quality, is not inferior to the best West India description. It may not be generally known that in Venezuela very little slave labour in the production of sugar is employed, that institution being nearly abolished ; and which, in a very few years will be looked upon as a thing of the past.

The Morning Chronicle contains an account of a new mode of manufacturing sugar, the introduction of which into the West Indies cannot fail to arrest the declension of property and produce in that part of the world. The new processes are fourfold in their character, comprising, first, a new mode of obtaining the saccharine juice from the cane: secondly, a new mode of defecating and filtering the juice so obtained ; thirdly, the boiling and concentrating of the juice; and fourthly, the crystallisation and final curing of the sugar. The varied processes are to be seen at a model sugar house, at the works of Mr. Bessemer, Baxter-house, Obi St. Pancras Road, London. By the first improvement, in the construction of the cane-press, a difference in the yield of the cane is obtained, as compared with the old rolling mill, of about 20 per cent. In the new machine the pressing tubes are reduced in length from 30 inches to 12, the first four of which are parallel, and three inches wide þÿ the next four inches of their length being taper, and terminating with a width of but I \ inch, the smaller contracted point extending as far as the exit end of the tube. By this change of. in the " magas" occupying the tubes is form the entire removal of the elasticity removed, and after the cane has been collapsed by the severe pressure, audits breadth at the same time gradually lessened, every fibre and cell is made to assume new relative positions þÿ not one remains unruptured, and an increased

quantity of the juice is consequently expelled at the trough. In addition to this advantage, there is obviously a more equal distribution of power in each reous volution of the or machine; the deleteri- chlorophyl, colouring matter, of the outer portion of the cane is not expelled with the juice, as in the ordinary apparatus; the machine may be more easily fed, and weighs considerably less than rolling machines generally in use. The juice when expelled from the cane is unavoidably mixed with numberless minute fragments ol cellular tissue, albumen, and other extraneous matters, which, i( not speedily removed, tend to produce the acidification of the liquid. At this stage comes in the second of the processes invented by Mr. Bessemer. The present mode of defecation and filtration consists in raising the temperature of the liquor to 150 deg. Fall., when, a quantity of lime is thrown in for the purpose of neutralising the free acid, and assisting in the coagulation of the albumen ; the temperature is increased to 180 deg. Fall., when, after allowing time for settling, the scum is reinto the " grand" copper, where it is sub- moved, and the clear liquor drawn off jected to a boiling heat, when the feculent and other albuminous matters arc kept constantly removed from its surface. The more completely these impurities are removed, the greater will be the brightness and value of the finished product. In the new process the juice passes through a wire strainer di-

rect from the spout of the mill into the clarifiers, where it is raised to boiling heat by the application of steam, at which temperature it is kept for about three minutes, by which time the whole of its albuminous constituents and feculent matters will have been coagulated and chemically separated, but will, of mechanically mixed, and, in the form of light flock, pervade

the entire bulk of the fluid. iThese substances are then effectually removed by a process similar to that employed in the manufacture of paper. A drum of about two feet in diameter and from four to five feet in length is made to revolve slowly vessel. This drum is covered with fine in a small semi-circular tray or wire cloth, through which the water forces its way, leaving a muddy coating of extraneous matters on the outer side, which, coming in contact as it revolves with a fixed scraper, similar in principle to the ' doctor" employed in calico printing, is made to fall off in a state something like dry mud into a receptacle prepared for it. The process is self-acting. It takes in its own supply of foul liquor from an elevated cistern, delivers the clear juice into the evaporating pan, and discharges the refuse as we have already stated. Up to this stage the advantages obtained must be evident to all who are acquainted with this interesting branch of manufacture. The liquor being received direct from the press, avoids the necessity of the use of liquor pumps; the clarifiers, not being used as subsiding vessels, are not required to be so large; the loss of juice in the removal of the scum and in the sediment is pre- vented ; the use of the " mont-jus is rendered unnecessary; the coagulation of the albuminous matter is more rapidly obtained; the evaporating process may follow immediately after the pressing of the canes; and finally, the selfcleansing filter performs its work much

better than any continuous process of skimming, and renders unnecessary that watchful attendance which is now so imperatively necessary in order to obtain the required brightness and colour of the sugar. The saving of manual labour by these improvements is self-evident. On the various modes of boiling and concentrating the juice at present in use, whether by a series of semiglobular pans, the vacuum pan, Gadsden's pan, or the apparatus of Mr. Crossley or Mr. Schroder, it is not necessary' now to all of them being the same þÿ speak, the principle involved that in one and of evaporating the fluid front the saccharine matter. The inventor of the process now under consideration, contends that, in all the existing arrangements lor the separation of the water from the sugar, boiling under any form, or the use of surfaces or pipes healed by steam, must he totally excluded, if the formation of molasses is to he prevented. It is a well-established fact that a thermometer placed in a solution heated hv steam or the direct action of fire furnishes no indication of the temperature to which the liquid is exposed, as a vast amount of latent heat is absorbed by Huids in their formation into steam. To the forgetfulness of this simple fact are to be traced many of the fatal mistakes at present connected with the manufacture of sugar. Thus, while the temperature of the syrup during ebullition in a vacuum-pan indicates as low perhaps as 180 degrees Fahrenheit, the copper worm, against which portions of the sugar are constant-

ly brought into contact, is equal to and often above 220 degrees Fahrenheit ; the consequence of which is the destruction of the colour, and an injury to the crystallising powers of the sugar. By an arrangement which Mr. Bessemer terms a hot-air evaporator, the concentration of saccharine fluids may now, however, be effected without the slightest injury to colour or quality, and in an increased quantity. This apparatus consists of a tank of thin plate iron, of about 10 feet by 8 feet, and 2J feet in depth, which has a false bottom, curved so as to form two parallel segments of a cylinder. Above these

At one end of the hollow drum, air, supplied by a blowing fan, and heated to 150 degrees by passing along a flue, is made to enter, þÿ\vhich escapes through the holes in the drum in a radial direction, and sweeps like the hot breath of the simoom over the wet surfaces of the various tevolving blades, absorbs the moisture thus exposed to its action, and passes off in an invisible vapour. Upwards of six thousand square feet of evaporating surface is thus obtained in the small space of 10 feet by 8 feet. The sc rews make about eight revolutions per minute, and as they revolve, the more concentrated portions of the fluid are washed off as tliev descend into the fluid, and fresh portions are being constantly brought up on the surfaces <>t the screw, to he in like manner subjected to the hot-air blast. Finally, after three or four hours, the whole ot the surplus liquor is carried oft ; the remaining fluid is sufficiently concentrated, and assumes a thick gelatinous appearance ; and the screw, made to revolve in the opposite direction, expels the solution from the tank ready for the process of crystallisa-

tion. By this process the sugar is net at any time exposed to a hotter surface than 140 degrees, no boiling consequently takes place, no slca is formed, and not one grain of crvstallisable sugar is converted into molasses. The entire cost of fuel for evaporation is saved, the waste heat of the chimney and waste stt'nm of ill. fiijririP ..!,»»»« «-,ri j.li.yred, and the apparatus costs less than the ordinary vapour pans ; it can he worked with a small amount of wind or water power. Three hogsheads of sugar, it is stated, can lie obtained where two only are now produced, whilst the quality will will taste, and he superior in colour and be perfectly free from molasses. The separation of the crystals from the mother liquor in which they are found is effected in a most ingenious and efficient manner by the use of the air pump. The transformation from the most repulsive and unwholesome-looKing black sugar into a fine white sugar is completed in one-seventh of a second by this process. The principle adopted " gassing" lace is precisely that employed in þÿ an operation resorted to for the purpose of removing the minute filaments of cotton adlicr ng to the surface of the fabric. I the case of the crystals of sugar, a thin film of fluid matter is required to he removed from the surface of the crystal, and this is effected by bringing it in contact with water þÿ a material which would as quickly dissolve the crystal itself, as the flame of the gas would destroy the delicate and fragile web of the bobbin net. How

can the water he thus brought into contact with the sugar for such a short period, and in such a manner as only to remove the outer coating of molasses, and leave the crystal uninjured? The process is a very simple one. A table of nine feet in circumference is made to revolve eight times per minute, having a coating of sugar spread over it to the depth of half art inch, a and which over of 72 conse- leet quently moves one space per minute. At pari of its revolution the table is made to pass under a pipe <|f' two inches in diameter, from which a shower of water is falling, and as the pipe is but one-sixth of a foot in

diameter, and the table passes it at the rate of '2 feet per minute, it follows that each portion which comes under the falling water will be retained only 1-432 of a minute in each revolution. This table being covered with thin brass wire gaiiae, lias placed immediately under it a vacuum chamber, into whicn the falling water, carrying with it the semifluid coating of molasses, is drawn as the table revolves, the crystallised sugar remains on the surface pure and white, and is delivered by a scraper into the hogshead placed for its reception.
